#6127. Delta’s Amazon Leo Wi-Fi Plans Face Uncertainty After Rocket Failure

Inflight Wi-Fi is currently undergoing quite the glow-up, thanks to the widespread rollout of Starlink Wi-Fi. Not only are most airlines offering this service for free, but it also represents a massive upgrade in terms of speeds.

While carriers like United, American, Southwest, and Alaska, are all rolling out Starlink Wi-Fi, Delta is countering the trend, and went with Amazon Leo, which is Amazon’s competitor to Starlink. This has of course made quite some headlines, due to Elon Musk’s public ridicule of Delta, plus what Delta CEO Ed Bastian reportedly said behind closed doors. Along those lines, there’s some potentially bad news for Delta.

On Sunday, November 15, 2026, a Vulcan rocket operated by United Launch Alliance (ULA), a joint venture between Boeing and Lockheed Martin, failed about 10 minutes after lifting off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. This was the first mission failure in ULA’s roughly 20-year history, and the company has issued the following statement in response to this:

Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit.

Every flight generates data, and every flight teaches us something. Since the anomaly just occurred, we don’t have any specific data yet to understand what occurred today.

ULA exists to provide assured access to space for our nation and for the customers who depend on us. That purpose is why we take on some of the hardest missions in spaceflight, and why we hold ourselves to the standard of mission success. Today, we did not meet that standard.

We will work closely with our customer and other appropriate organizations to find the cause, determine the appropriate corrective action, and return to flight as quickly as possible.

ULA is committed to full transparency with our customers, and they will have visibility into the investigation process, which utilizes rigorous methodology and corrective action.

We will provide further updates when new information becomes available.

BREAKING: The Vulcan Rocket of United Launch Alliance (Lockheed Martin and Boeing) suffered total mission failure minutes after launchAll 40 Amazon Leo satellites onboard were destroyed pic.twitter.com/NskOOy8uAW

This isn’t about the loss of 40 satellites as such, as that’s only a tiny percentage of the satellites that were supposed to be deployed as part of Amazon Leo, across dozens of missions. Instead, the issue is that this will now delay future launches, while an investigation is performed, improvements are made, etc.

Prior to this, 398 satellites had already been deployed for Amazon Leo, across 14 launches, making up around 12% of the 3,236 satellites that are needed for global coverage.

This rocket failure is absolutely a setback for the rollout of Amazon Leo, though it remains to be seen just how much of a delay it represents. Amazon has released a statement saying it remains confident that ULA will learn from the mission and deliver on their long term plans.

We know that Amazon Leo was targeted for an initial service rollout before the end of 2026 in select regions, with a more widespread introduction in the months that follow.

Rockets are far from my area of expertise, but based on my understanding from those who know more than I do, it seems that this likely represents a delay of several months to the program, at an absolute minimum, if not more. As you’d expect, a thorough investigation needs to be performed, any learnings need to be implemented, etc.

Keep in mind that JetBlue was supposed to introduce Amazon Leo as of 2027, and Delta was supposed to introduce Amazon Leo as of 2028. I think it’s safe to say that the timeline looks worse today than it did 24 hours ago.

One of the risks with picking a service that’s still in development is that the timeline is really quite fluid, and this is an example of that. Delta has of course made quite the headlines over its lack of selecting Starlink, and I imagine this will only make matters worse for the airline.

United expects to have Starlink on all planes by the end of 2027, while Delta was only going to start introducing Amazon Leo on less than half of its planes as of 2028. So the airline was already at a disadvantage there, and that disadvantage has just grown even bigger.

A Vulcan rocket operated by United Launch Alliance (ULA) suffered a failure on Sunday, as it was on a mission to deploy dozens of Amazon Leo satellites. While this was only a small part of the overall rollout of this, the failure will absolutely delay additional rocket launches, which are needed to get this network functioning. This was the first mission failure in ULA’s roughly 20-year history.

It’s anyone’s guess how much of a delay it will cause for the introduction of Amazon Leo, and what impact that will have on Delta and JetBlue. It’s absolutely certain that the timeline looks worse now than 24 hours ago, though we don’t know much more as of now.

#6126. JSX Adds New Route From NY

JSX is launching a new nonstop route between the New York metro area and North Texas.

Starting Feb. 17, the public charter service will connect Teterboro Airport in New Jersey with Dallas Love Field. Flights will operate daily.

The service will be available only to members of the carrier’s free loyalty program, Club JSX.

“New York City and Dallas are two of America’s most influential business and cultural centers, and we believe traveling between them should be as seamless as the opportunities that connect them,” JSX CEO Alex Wilcox said in a news release. “As we continue expanding our network, our focus remains on giving customers something increasingly rare in air travel: more of their time back. With this new daily service, we’re bringing the simplicity, comfort, and convenience of JSX to one of the country’s most important travel corridors.”

JSX added service to Teterboro, which it markets as New York City, in 2025. It also serves Westchester County Airport, located just north of New York.

For years, the travel industry has been embracing artificial intelligence, using it to make websites easier to digest — and even generate personalized recommendations. Now, it has become an invaluable tool for travelers searching for the best Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals.

Experts told TPG that using AI can make the start of trip planning feel less daunting and more natural. In fact, travelers can ask for a list of hotels within a certain budget range, and that happen to be close to things like public transport or have perks like free breakfast, said Melanie Fish, a travel expert at Expedia.

“Instead of starting with a long list of filters, travelers can tell [sites like] Expedia or Hotels.com what they have in mind, in their own words,” Fish said. “AI can help them explore hotel options, compare what matters and narrow the choices.”

At Hotels.com, the company offers a “Natural Language Search” for Black Friday travel deals, allowing travelers to search for things like “‘Four nights in Barcelona in May on sale for Black Friday or Travel Tuesday,’ and get hotels offering up to 50 [percent] off,” Fish said.

Ian Ackland, the managing director for the Americas at Booking.com, recommended travelers start their prompt with the kind of trip they want, rather than just searching by the discounts that pop up post-Thanksgiving. That’s because what constitutes a “good deal” may mean more than simply a cheap rate.

“Share your destination, dates, budget and the details that matter, like breakfast, family space or walkable restaurants,” Ackland said. “The more specific you are, the more useful the results can be. A good deal is one that fits the trip, not one that’s simply the lowest price.”

Related: How AI is transforming the future of travel

It can also be used for side-by-side comparisons of different hotel options, said Google spokesperson Sarah Armstrong. At Google, the AI assistant Gemini can pull everything from base rates to estimated taxes, resort fees, cancellation policies and more.

The AI tool can also save time by continuing to work in the background with things like price alerts while travelers focus on other things.

“When you're ready to secure your room, Auto Browse in Gemini in Chrome can take the wheel,” Armstrong said. “Working right from the Chrome side panel, Gemini can navigate travel sites, fill in your dates and select your room options then pause safely at the checkout screen so you can review the final details before paying.”

That said, AI isn’t full proof. That’s especially true with Black Friday deals since prices can change quickly and promotional terms vary, Fish said.

“Tools like Claude and ChatGPT can be a useful shortcut, but travelers should treat its recommendations as a starting point, not the final source of truth,” Fish said. “Potential pitfalls include outdated or incomplete pricing, missed taxes and fees, limited availability, incorrect details about amenities or cancellation policies, and recommendations that don’t reflect the traveler’s priorities.”

Ackland said Booking.com has worked with AI for over a decade, and ultimately, it “should help you make a decision, not leave you guessing about what you’ve booked.”

It is important to note while AI tools do “occasionally get things wrong,” Armstrong said, it won’t make purchases without permission. Nonetheless, “it's still smart to review the key details like dates, prices, and cancellation rules before hitting confirm.”

Thankfully, Fish said picking whether travelers use AI or a traditional search engine doesn't have to be “an either-or choice.”

“AI is particularly useful for inspiration and discovery,” Fish said, “while traditional search and trusted travel platforms… remain the best places to confirm live prices, availability, sale terms, guest reviews and cancellation policies — and to complete the booking.”

#6124. Condor Asks Passengers To Share Magazines To Save On Fuel Costs

It’s obviously a tough time for many airlines around the globe, given the impact that higher jet fuel prices are having on economics, in an industry with razor thin margins. Along those lines, German airline Condor is looking for all kinds of way to save on fuel costs… including reducing the number of inflight magazines onboard!

aeroTELEGRAPH flags how as of November 1, 2026, German airline Condor has slashed the number of inflight shopping magazines it has onboard flights. Instead of each passenger having their own inflight shopping magazine:

The airline has confirmed that the goal is “to reduce the weight on board and thus fuel consumption,” and it’s pointed out how the inflight shopping magazine is also available digitally, via the inflight entertainment system. These inflight shopping magazines have both the food & drinks available for purchase, as well as duty free items.

Initially this is being viewed as a trial, and after winter, the airline will decide whether or not to continue with this policy.

Over the years, we’ve seen a good number of airlines eliminate duty free sales and inflight magazines, with the primary motivation being to reduce the weight of the aircraft. However, it’s definitely a bit unusual to see an airline put a magazine at some seats, but not others. After all, some people may prefer a physical magazine, so are you supposed to ask your seat mate if you can borrow it, or how does that work?!

I am curious if this leads to a reduction in onboard sales. After all, passengers onboard flights are a pretty captive audience, and might browse a magazine out of boredom. I mean, just look at SkyMall, in all of its former glory. Did anyone really need the world’s largest wine glass, or a bigfoot garden statue? Nope! But if you’re bored enough, you might be convinced of some pretty wild things!

Condor isn’t stopping at inflight magazines when it comes to trying to find ways to reduce the weight of aircraft. This is part of a larger project at the airline, with the goal of operating flights as efficiently as possible, with as much resource conservation as possible.

In order to find additional cost saving measures, the airline is undergoing a cabin clearing process, as it’s described. This involves removing all movable items from the aircraft, inspecting them, and then deciding if they’re needed anymore. Of course safety equipment is the one exception.

Realistically, I can’t imagine there’s all that much that can be removed anymore, without cutting some very basic amenities on long haul flights. After all, it’s not the 1970s, and it’s not like there are endless amenities onboard for passengers.

German airline Condor is asking passengers to share inflight shopping magazines, as part of an initiative intended to reduce the weight of aircraft. While it goes without saying that a single magazine doesn’t lead to a huge increase in fuel burn, when you multiply it by the number of magazines, the number of flights an aircraft makes, and the number of aircraft in the fleet, it sure can add up.

While eliminating things like seat back magazines is nothing new, the concept of sharing magazines is a new one for me. Obviously Condor wants it both ways — it still wants to be able to make money selling things, but doesn’t want the weight of one magazine per person.

I am curious if this test proves successful, or if this leads to a material reduction in sales.

What’s your take on Condor’s cost saving initiative?

#6123. T-19A Kestrel: Meet The US Air Force Academy's New Unlimited Aerobatic Aircraft For Cadets

On November 12, four new composite planes swept low over the Cadet Wing assembled at the US Air Force Academy in Colorado. The flight marked the official arrival of the T-19A Kestrel light trainer at Davis Airfield in Colorado Springs. Instead of wading through decades of defense bureaucracy and drawn-out congressional appropriations, USAFA secured its next-generation aerobatic aircraft in just 10 months, cutting through red tape with the help of a private donor group led by Andrew McKenna.

The T-19A is a derivative of the commercial GB1 GameBird. By skipping the traditional procurement, leadership bypassed the budget overruns and timeline slips that have paralyzed programs like the Boeing T-7A Red Hawk. The lightweight plane is purpose-built for agility thanks to its designer, German aerobatic champion Philipp Steinbach. He is a co-founder of Game Aerospace Composites in Bentonville, Arkansas, which produces the off-the-shelf civilian variant certified to pull a staggering load of ten G-forces.

The Kestrel went from concept to delivery in 10 months using $3 million in private donations, whereas the Red Hawk has spent over a decade in development using billions in taxpayer funds and still faces multi-year delays. The T-19A will fill a major gap in modern USAFA flight training by giving cadets early exposure to high-G, unlimited aerobatics and complex energy management before they ever step into Undergraduate Pilot Training.

The T-19A, or GB1 GameBird, is the only American-built two-seat aircraft approved for Unlimited-category competition aerobatics. Its all-carbon monocoque airframe lacks traditional mechanical wing-attach joints, relying on a continuous composite spar cured inside an autoclave. This gives the plane an operating empty weight of roughly 1,290 pounds (585 kg) while enabling symmetric flight loads of up to 10-G at its aerobatic maximum limit.

Under the hood, a 583-cubic-inch Lycoming AEIO-580-B1A flat-six piston engine delivers 303 horsepower (226 kW) to a four-blade composite MT-Propeller system. An inverted oil and fuel system keeps the engine running under sustained negative-g flight and zero-g push-overs. Cadets command the airframe from tandem seats equipped with Garmin G3X Touch glass displays, combining edge-of-envelope stick-and-rudder forces with modern electronic flight screens before stepping into standard turboprops.

To make the transition, USAFA pulled six active-duty instructor pilots from the 306th Flying Training Group to stand up the first training cadre. These officers will shape a new syllabus to train cadets and establish a demonstration and competition team. The initiative comes as the wider military struggles with a persistent shortfall of roughly 2,000 operational pilots, forcing leadership to seek shortcuts to build stick-and-rudder skills earlier in pilot development.

The Academy's existing fleet jumps from unpowered TG-16A gliders and basic T-53A/T-41D piston trainers straight to the UPT's T-6A Texan II turboprops after graduation. USAF Chief of Staff General Ken Wilsbach and Academy Superintendent Lt. Gen. Paul Moga secured the four airframes thanks to a $3 million donation coordinated by philanthropist Andrew McKenna. Meanwhile, the USAFA paid $400,000 in operational funds for initial tooling, spares, and flight gear, along with a projected annual operating budget of $1 million to maintain the fleet.

The Kestrel will act as an intermediate high-performance step, teaching cadets how to manage high power-to-weight ratios, rapid throttle response, and aggressive energy management. Standard trainers are built for stability and prohibit extreme maneuvers. Because the Kestrel is certified for unlimited aerobatics, instructors can deliberately put cadets into inverted spins, vertical stalls, and disorienting attitudes, teaching them instinctive recovery skills that directly prevent real-world loss-of-control accidents.

The Air Force is facing a persistent pilot deficit and needs to push students through UPT faster without lowering standards. By giving top cadets advanced stick-and-rudder proficiency during their junior and senior years at the Academy, they arrive at UPT needing fewer remedial rides and moving through the syllabus faster. Additionally, building an aerobatic competition team around the Kestrel will push the selected cadets to fly under public scrutiny with the precision and discipline they will further refine in operational flying squadrons.

How the pay checks stack up in the world's top air forces.

Operating the Kestrel at the USAFA in Colorado Springs comes with real performance trade-offs. The Academy's Davis Airfield sits at an elevation of 6,572 feet (2,003 meters), and summer heat often makes the air feel like it is over 9,000 feet (2,743 meters). That means the T-19A's non-turbocharged engine loses roughly 22% to 26% of its power. That thinner mountain air requires longer takeoff runs and leaves pilots with less excess engine power during demanding maneuvers.

Weight limits create another hurdle for daily operations, as the Kestrel can weigh up to 2,200 pounds (998 kg) for standard point-to-point flights. Its maximum takeoff rating for extreme 10-G aerobatics only applies at 1,940 pounds (880 kg) or less. Subtracting the plane's 1,290-pound (585 kg) empty weight leaves just 650 pounds (295 kg) for people, gear, and fuel. Once an instructor and a cadet strap in, only enough weight allowance remains for 25 to 30 gallons (95 to 114 liters) of fuel.

That limits intense flights to roughly 45 minutes, requiring ground crews to refuel and turn the planes around quickly between sorties. Moving cadets from unpowered gliders into a 200-knot (370 km/h) airplane is also a major operational adjustment. Because rapid spins and heavy G-forces can easily cause motion sickness or make new pilots lose track of which way is up, instructors must design a step-by-step program that gradually introduces cadets to the plane's capabilities.

The vintage wings still making fighter pilots decades later.

Built entirely from carbon fiber, the T-19A brings modern composite design to a general aviation field long dominated by traditional steel-tube frames. Even compared to the newer carbon-fiber Extra NG, the Kestrel weighs about 110 pounds (50 kg) less at an empty weight of 1,290 pounds (585 kg). Its wing and fuselage tanks also hold 81 gallons (307 liters) of fuel, giving it a cross-country range of over 1,000 nautical miles (1,852 kilometers).

In the air, the Kestrel reacts far faster than almost all other military trainers. The USAF's primary turboprop trainer, the Beechcraft T-6A Texan II, rolls at 180 degrees per second and handles forces between positive 7.0-G and negative 3.5-G. The Kestrel more than doubles that agility, rolling at 400 degrees per second while withstanding up to positive and negative 10-G.

Unlike older aerobatic planes, the Kestrel avoids the sluggish handling caused by a heavy nose-mounted radial engine. Its horizontally opposed Lycoming responds instantly, without the twisting-torque side effects of a radial engine during aggressive maneuvers. That instant throttle response also translates into blistering acceleration and vertical climb performance. Its power-to-weight ratio allows the Kestrel to take off in just 680 feet (207 meters) and climb at 4,200 feet per minute (1,280 meters per minute).

This sharp handling marks a major departure from the Academy’s existing T-53As, which are militarized Cirrus SR20s built to train for instrument flying rather than agility and dogfighting. The Kestrel bridges that gap, letting cadets practice inverted flight, vertical spins, and high-G recovery before they arrive at active-duty pilot training bases to begin the pipeline to the cockpit of a warplane.

The United States Air Force Academy operates 19 TG-16A gliders.

The T-19A's performance derives from its lightweight carbon-fiber fuselage built around a single, continuous spar that runs straight through the cabin floor. By dropping heavy metal wing joints, Game Aerospace saved weight while also making the 25.26-foot (7.70-meter) span wings strong enough to withstand extreme loads up to 15-G.

Up front, the engine spins a 74.8-inch (1,900 mm) German-made MT-Propeller built from a compressed wood core wrapped in a tough composite shell with stainless-steel leading edges. Because standard engines lose oil pressure when flying upside down, the Kestrel uses a specialized inverted oil system that keeps oil flowing smoothly between 55 and 95 psi (3.8 and 6.5 bar) at temperatures up to 245°F (118°C), even during violent tumbling maneuvers.

Instead of flexible steel cables that can stretch under heavy loads, the pilot's control stick connects to the wings and tail via rigid metal pushrods mounted on sealed bearings for instant, slop-free response. Small aerodynamic paddles beneath the wings help balance the large carbon ailerons so the stick stays light at speeds up to 175 knots (324 km/h), while tiny fins along the wing surface keep airflow smooth and prevent sudden wing stalls down to 60 knots (111 km/h).

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

The aircraft’s 83-gallon (314-liter) fuel system is divided to handle both long cross-country trips and intense aerobatics. For extreme maneuvering, pilots draw gas solely from a central 25-gallon (95-liter) fuselage tank fitted with a weighted, flexible pickup hose that moves around inside the tank to follow the fuel whether the plane is right-side up or inverted. Two 28.5-gallon (108-liter) wing tanks provide extra range for long flights, though pilots must keep them empty during high-G aerobatics to avoid putting extra stress on the wings.

#6122. Sexual harassment overhaul at a crossroads in the House

The leaders of an effort to overhaul how the House deals with sexual misconduct hope their proposal will see action before the end of the 119th Congress, though they’re split on the odds.

Rep. Kat Cammack, R-Fla., chair of the Republican Women’s Caucus, said legislative text is done and is being looked at by the relevant committees.

“Yes, absolutely,” she said when asked if the package would get a vote this year. “We’re shopping it now with the different committees, House Admin and Ethics, and waiting on their final feedback, which we should have actually this week.”

Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus, said she was still optimistic about getting it done, but stopped short of putting full faith in Republican leadership to get it over the finish line. The effort has been underway since May, when Cammack and Leger Fernández’s caucuses announced a partnership to propose changes after two members of the House resigned amid allegations of sexual misconduct.

Asked if she thought Speaker Mike Johnson would put the proposal on the floor during the busy lame-duck session, Leger Fernández laughed.

“Hopefully, that’s something that will happen, because you know the Republican Women’s Caucus had said they were optimistic before we left. I’m still optimistic,” she said.

The two groups have spent months holding dozens of meetings with staff, their own caucuses and male members of Congress, among others. Suggestions have included banning members of Congress from engaging in sexual relationships with any House staffer, not just those who work for them directly, and outlining penalties for violaters. Initially, the groups were expected to unveil their work by August recess, but that got pushed back as the House canceled weeks in session and as they cited a desire to get it right.

Cammack said she thinks Johnson “has been very sincere in his efforts on this.”

“That would be a tremendous disappointment” if he didn’t put it on the floor, she said when asked about the possibility. “I genuinely believe he cares about this issue.”

Leger Fernández said if it doesn’t get done by the end of the 119th Congress, she hopes some changes would be adopted under the rules package for the next Congress that Democrats bring forward in January. Such packages are typically adopted with party-line votes and give incoming majorities the chance to tweak how the House operates to their liking. While certain narrower proposals aimed at curbing sexual harassment could be written into House rules, others would need to pass both chambers and be enacted into law to take effect.

“We are going to move to make sure it is in the rules package, because we will be in charge next year,” Leger Fernández said. “But I would love for it to pass now, because that was a commitment that it be bipartisan.”

#6121. Welcome To One Mile At A Time, Daniel Ross! Here’s What’s Going On…

It’s a big day here at OMAAT, as I’m delighted to welcome our first full time contributor in the site’s nearly 19-year history. Let me start with a little bit of background, and then I’ll talk about Daniel Ross, who is joining the team. As a creature of habit, this feels like a whole new frontier, but I’m excited!

I’m incredibly fortunate that I’ve never had a “traditional” job — I started OMAAT my freshmen year of college as a hobby (after having been passionate about miles & points in my teens), and nearly 19 years later, that’s still what I get to do full time.

I’m blessed that I can wake up every day and cover an industry that I love. While OMAAT is a business that pays my bills, it has never been exclusively about maximizing profitability, coming up with some five-year business plan, or seeing what opportunities there are to sell. It’s also my hobby.

Now, the downside to this — at least if you ask my family — is that I also “work” seven days per week, 365 days per year. Other sites in the space that are this size might have one or two dozen contributors, but for me, that has never sounded very appealing. My passion is actually getting to cover the industry, rather than managing a huge group of people.

Let me be clear, I don’t do this alone, as I have two great people who do a ton of to work to handle everything in the background, much of which readers don’t see — Jeremy oversees business development (basically anything having to do with the business side of things), and Howie manages things related to credit cards and tech (which largely helps pay the bills!). I’m incredibly grateful for their contributions, because it allows me to focus on content.

In the past, I’ve had some part time contributors, and I also very much appreciate the contributions they’ve made. However, given the volume of content at OMAAT, it’s hard for that to make a meaningful difference in terms of workload, etc.

Recently I finally accepted the fact that it’s time to add a full time contributor. That’s not because I want to meaningfully change anything about the site in terms of the content mix, or because I want to step back from things. Quite to the contrary, it’s because I want to do the best possible job I can.

As many people can surely attest to, if you take pride in what you do (rather than just turning your site into an AI slop machine), it just takes a lot more effort than in the past to accomplish the same results, given how everything on the internet has shifted. Aside from spending time with family, this site and industry is basically my entire life — it’s not a means to an end, but the passion as such is the “end.”

So my hope is that by having someone join the team full time on the content front, I can actually put more time into the areas that I’d like to improve — engaging with the community, responding to comments and emails, etc. These are all things I’ve gotten very bad at, not due to a lack of caring, but due to a lack of hours in the day, especially as someone who has two small kids.

For that matter, I’m planning on imminently launching a new video series (which I wrote about over the summer), not to replace written content, but to complement it, as I think we have a unique angle for it. I just couldn’t carve out the time for that without getting some more help. So I’m finally no longer putting this off, and I’m ripping the band aid-off.

Let me emphasize that the goal here is to genuinely do a better job of providing useful and interesting content to community members, rather than anything else. This isn’t a “we’re cutting free food & drinks in economy due to customer feedback, it’s an enhancement” situation!

I’d like to welcome Daniel Ross to OMAAT, as he’s joining full time as of today! Daniel isn’t new to the miles & points world, as has he contributed to many sites over the years (The Points Guy, Business Insider, Upgraded Points, etc.), so odds are good that you may be familiar with him (and you can follow him at cometravelwithdan on Instagram).

Shortly Daniel will be publishing his first post introducing himself, but let me provide a little background on how this came to be, and how I envision this evolving.

I’ve actually never met Daniel before in person. I’ve always had respect for his work and think he has done a great job with writing, social media, video content, etc. We hadn’t connected until not that long ago, and hit it off.

When it comes to working with people, and especially adding them to the OMAAT team, I try to follow my gut, and I think Daniel will be a good fit. I know OMAAT readers value opinions, analysis, and someone with interesting takes, and I think Daniel checks all those boxes. For example, he was just telling me about Aerolineas Argentinas’ quirky baggage allowance, so I’m excited for the expanded content coverage, as that’s something I would’ve never written about (I’m more into covering Air Côte d’Ivoire’s insane first class carry-on allowance).

One of the specific reasons I don’t want a dozen contributors is because I think it’s important for people to have a unique voice, and for readers to get to know that, and I think people will enjoy hearing Daniel’s takes on things.

Daniel also does a great job with social media and video content, which is something that I’ve historically struggled with. My general philosophy is that if I can’t do something right, I won’t do it at all, and that basically sums up the OMAAT strategy for social media up until now. 😉 I think Daniel strikes the unique balance of being interesting without being obnoxious and clickbaity, and I appreciate that.

So, what exactly will Daniel be doing at OMAAT? This is very much a “we’re going to evolve together on this” situation, given the initiatives I’ve had in mind for some time:

Transparency is important to me, and Daniel is someone who understands how “particular” the OMAAT community is. 😉 Obviously the OMAAT community is very much about written content, so that’s why I think it’s important that this is where he focuses to begin with, since that’s the medium people are most familiar with. Then we’ll see where things go from there…

It’s an exciting (scary?) day here at OMAAT, as Daniel Ross is joining the team, as the first full time contributor of the site in its nearly 19 year history. I’m excited, and the goal is to add someone with a unique and interesting voice, to expand coverage on things, etc.

My hope is also that it frees up a little more time for me, so I can focus a bit more on the community aspect of things. In the long run, you can also expect a bit more of a focus on video and social media, but we’re starting with what we know here!

I’m excited about this, and Daniel will have a post soon introducing himself. Thanks to everyone for their patience, and stay tuned!

PS: For those wondering about the British Airways 747 featured image, it’s because I noticed Daniel had that as his model plane in the background behind his desk during our video calls, so we’ll throw him that Easter egg. 😉

#6120. How Are Hotels Paid When You Redeem Points, And For Elite Perks?

There’s a real thrill to redeeming points for stays at luxury properties, and getting outsized value. I’m sure many people have wondered about the economics of that. How much is the hotel getting reimbursed for your stay? Who is paying for any elite perks that you receive? Does the hotel care if you redeemed points or not? Let’s talk about those various points in this post…

The major global hotel groups (Hilton, Hyatt, IHG, Marriott, etc.) don’t own a vast majority of their properties. Instead, the companies have an asset light strategy, and have management or franchise contracts for the individual properties.

In some cases, large investment firms own hotels, and they may have properties belonging to all kinds of brands. In other cases, a hotel may even be family owned.

The way the major hotel groups make money is primarily through fees (they’re also increasingly directly monetizing their loyalty programs, but that’s a whole different topic). There’s typically an initial fee to open the hotel, and then on top of that, there are fees on ongoing revenue. The ongoing fees typically fall into one of two categories (and they’re typically a percentage of revenue):

Then any upside (or downside) typically falls with the hotel owner. So the major hotel groups are making money, regardless of whether a hotel is raking in the cash or hemorrhaging money.

Now, one of the reasons that consumers flock to certain hotel groups is because of their loyalty programs, which are massive marketing machines. A big part of the value proposition of these loyalty programs is the ability to redeem points.

As you’d expect, those points are redeemed centrally through the program, and then the loyalty program has to “buy” that room from the hotel. After all, the hotel owner wants to be compensated for each head in a bed, especially since they’re already paying a system fund fee, to fund these perks. That brings us to the question of how hotels are reimbursed…

As you’d expect, hotel groups don’t publicly disclose how they reimburse their properties when members redeem points. However, over the years we’ve been able to get some insights into this.

Sometimes guests are given folios that are actually intended for the loyalty program, while in other cases the reimbursement rates showed up online when they weren’t supposed to.

While the exact reimbursement policies differ by program, here’s the general concept:

So I’m totally making this up here, but if a hotel is charging $400 on a particular night, maybe the loyalty program would pay $80 for that room if occupancy is under 90%, while it might be paying $350 if occupancy is over 90%.

Note that the number of points you redeem for a stay doesn’t directly determine reimbursement for a hotel. In other words, a hotel doesn’t get paid X amount per redeemed point. Similarly, if a program offers a fifth night free on award redemptions, the hotel is getting reimbursed for all five nights, as it’s the loyalty program incurring the cost there.

Instead, points redemption rates are set by the loyalty program, and are intended to reflect the cost incurred by the program. That’s why in many cases you’ll find that redemption rates don’t correlate directly to how much a property would cost in cash, but rather also factor in average occupancy at a property.

A hotel loyalty program would probably rather you redeem your points at a $1,000 per night hotel that’s 50% full, rather than a $500 per night hotel that’s 95% full, because the latter redemption will cost the program more. Hotel loyalty programs use historical data to determine points pricing, and the costs they incur.

Let me actually give a real example from a recent stay. I recently redeemed points for a two night stay at a Wyndham Rewards property, at the cost of 30,000 points per night. The folio I was sent accidentally had the amount Wyndham had to pay, rather than the amount I had to pay.

Even though I was paying the same number of points both nights, the hotel was being reimbursed around $87 for one night, and $184 for the next night. Funny enough, while sitting in the lobby working the first morning, I overheard one front desk agent tell the other that they were fully sold out the following night, so that tracks. The first night was being reimbursed at a reduced rate, while the second night was being reimbursed based on something closer to the average daily rate.

If you have elite status with a hotel loyalty program, how does taking advantage of elite perks factor into this when redeeming points? Who pays for breakfast? Who pays for suite upgrades? Who pays for waived destination fees and parking?

The answer is that “it depends,” though here are a few general considerations:

As you can see, funding elite benefits is a combined effort between the loyalty program and hotels.

For those curious, generally individual hotels don’t know how you earned your elite status. So it doesn’t matter to them if you earned it through actual hotel stays, or just by holding onto a credit card. Presumably a front desk agent could look at your stay history, but they typically wouldn’t have any reason to do so, in this context.

This is a loaded question, and there’s obviously no single right or wrong answers. A few thoughts, though.

Hotel staff are trained by corporate to treat guests redeeming points the same way as those paying cash. Many hotel groups even train front desk staff to thank people for redeeming their points, since it reflects engagement in the program. Officially, you should expect exactly the same treatment as if you paid cash, and you absolutely shouldn’t feel sheepish about the fact that you didn’t pay cash for your stay.

Now, in practice that might not always be how things play out. There’s sometimes a back and forth between hotel owners and hotel groups. Hotel owners often want it both ways — they want the power of the major hotel group distribution channels and loyalty programs, without actually incurring the costs associated with it, whether it’s complimentary upgrades, points redemptions, or a decent breakfast.

Will you sometimes find a hotel that’s perhaps a bit condescending if you redeem points and have an issue? Absolutely, but it’s not how it should be, and it’s the exception rather than the norm. Some may remember my stay at the Aegon Mykonos, at the time a Marriott Autograph Collection property (the hotel has since… mysteriously disappeared?).

Long story short, I was downgraded despite using a confirmed upgrade, and the manager was completely unapologetic about it, and was unwilling to do anything meaningful. One of his defenses was that I was staying “complimentary,” and therefore shouldn’t be complaining.

The hotel industry is complex, given the various parties involved, from the hotel group to the individual hotel owners. Hopefully the above is a useful rundown of how reimbursement works when redeeming points. The important thing to understand is that hotels get paid a lot more when you’re redeeming points if the property is full.

When redeeming points, you definitely shouldn’t feel sheepish about it. You earned your stay, and the reason hotels belonging to major loyalty programs are able to command a revenue premium is because of the points and loyalty perks they offer.

What’s your take on how hotels are reimbursed for award stays? And do you feel like you’ve ever been treated differently when redeeming points?

#6119. Frontier Cancels Massive 17 International Routes: See Full List Now

Journalist – Aaron is an aviation and travel journalist with 14 years of experience in the travel and tourism industry. His background spans airport operations, aviation infrastructure, and travel consulting, having worked with global organizations across New Zealand, Europe, and North America. Combining industry expertise with firsthand travel experience across more than 52 countries and five continents, Aaron covers airlines, airports, aviation policy, and the wider travel sector. He is based in Canterbury, New Zealand. His work has been published in Simple Flying and featured by MSN, SAM CHUI Aviation & Travel, EIN News, Pakistan Defence, and Climate Depot.

Denver-based Frontier Airlines has rapidly cut a total of 16 international routes from its network this year, with Atlanta (ATL), one of the airline's major bases, losing a total of eight routes overall. These network changes have taken place between March and August 2026.

Data from Cirium, an aviation analytics company, shows that the budget airline has reconfigured its international operations. It is redeploying aircraft on more lucrative domestic or other international routes following a difficult year for airlines in the face of high fuel prices and other operational demands. This data has been reviewed against 2026 and 2027 flight schedules.

Frontier is the second-largest operator at Atlanta. However, it is still just a marginal player when compared to Delta, which calls Atlanta home. Frontier operates around 6% of all flights from Atlanta, according to the airport's website. The airline trimmed eight nonstop international routes from the airport in April of this year.

These affected services to Puerto Vallarta (PVR), San José del Cabo (SJD), Santo Domingo (SDQ), Nassau (NAS), Aruba (AUA), Providenciales (PLS), St Maarten (SXM), and San Pedro Sula (SAP). This leaves Frontier with a network of 40 domestic and six year-round international destinations from Atlanta.

The remaining five year-round services from Atlanta to Cancún (CUN), Guatemala City (GUA), Montego Bay (MBJ), San José, Costa Rica (SJO), and San Salvador (SAL). There is also a seasonal link to Punta Cana (PUJ).

Earlier this year, Denver (DEN) lost two international services served by Frontier. The airline withdrew its operations to San José del Cabo (SJD) from the Colorado airport in March, while Denver to Puerto Vallarta (PVR) lost its international link in April. This was followed by Charlotte (CLT) also losing its international route to Cancún (CUN) after the airline pulled service on the city pair in April.

This leaves the airline with no international routes from Charlotte. Now, it only has domestic flights to Baltimore (BWI), Chicago–O'Hare (ORD), Dallas/Fort Worth (DFW), Denver, Detroit (DTW), Fort Lauderdale (FLL), Houston–Intercontinental (IAH), Miami (MIA), New York–LaGuardia (LGA), Orlando (MCO), Philadelphia (PHL), San Juan (SJU), and Tampa (TPA).

Frontier's international route from Raleigh/Durham (RDU) to Cancún was also lost in May. Meanwhile, Orlando's link to St Maarten (SXM) was axed in summer, after the airline pulled the pin in August.

Atlanta loses multiple leisure routes while competitors like Delta expand to absorb sunseeking travelers from the hub.

The decision to consolidate a number of international routes was also seen in both Chicago and Miami, with Frontier terminating two services from each city. Chicago Midway (MDW) lost its service to Cancún in April, while O'Hare (ORD) lost its link to Punta Cana (PUJ) in the Dominican Republic.

This leaves Frontier with 23 domestic routes from O'Hare, and a further nine domestic routes from Midway. Frontier is the second-largest airline at Chicago Midway, the city's second busiest airport after O'Hare. While Southwest operates more than 91% of all flights at Midway, Frontier served over half a million passengers between June 2025 and May 2026, accounting for 3% of all traffic.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

Miami (MIA) is the final airport to have lost Frontier international services in this analysis, with the airline cutting international flights to Santo Domingo (SDQ) and San Salvador (SAL). Both cuts were made in April. These leave the Florida airport with 20 domestic year-round services by the airline and three international routes, which include Guatemala City (GUA) served year-round and two seasonal links to Punta Cana and San Pedro Sula.

#6118. Rep. Ken Calvert wins all-Republican race in California

Rep. Ken Calvert defeated Rep. Young Kim in a redrawn Southern California district that pitted the two Republicans against one another.

Calvert was leading his rival by 7 points Monday night when The Associated Press called the race for California’s 40th District with more than 70 percent of the vote in.

Calvert, who chairs the powerful House Defense Appropriations Subcommittee, is the longest-serving Republican in the California delegation, first winning election to Congress in 1992.

The race was reshaped by the Golden State’s new voter-approved House map, drawn by state Democrats in response to mid-decade redistricting by Texas Republicans. The new map dismantled Calvert’s 41st District in Riverside County, transforming it into a safely blue Democratic seat in the Los Angeles area. That prompted him to run for the redrawn 40th District, which included a sizable percentage of his current constituents.

The rare intraparty general election was possible because Calvert and Kim finished in the top two slots in the state’s June primary. Under the California system, all candidates run on the same primary ballot, with the top two vote-getters, regardless of party, advancing to November.

Calvert had already declared victory last week, saying on social media that there was “no greater honor than serving my neighbors and our communities in Congress.”

Kim’s defeat is the second of her congressional career — she lost her initial bid during the 2018 blue wave before winning election to the House two years later.

In her concession message, Kim singled out California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom, who led the redistricting effort last year that targeted five Republican-held districts. Democrats flipped all five seats last week.

“It’s unfortunate that Gavin Newsom’s political redistricting scheme forced two Republican members from Congress into this race,’’ she said in a statement.

The race between was marked by rancor, with Calvert alleging that Kim was not a true conservative and supported higher taxes. Kim accused Calvert of growing rich off stock trades over his decades in Washington.

Calvert will serve in a delegation with a dramatically smaller GOP presence next year, with Democrats likely to hold 48 of California’s 52 House seats. Just two other California Republicans – Reps. Vince Fong and Tom McClintock – have been reelected so far, while a third, Rep. Jay Obernolte, narrowly leads his Democratic challenger in an as-yet-uncalled race.

The Calvert-Kim battle was not the only all-party November clash in California, with several districts featuring matchups between two Democrats.

One incumbent has already been unseated, with Rep. Jimmy Gomez losing to fellow Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres in the Los Angeles-area 34th District, according to The Associated Press.

Two other blue-on-blue contests in Northern California remained uncalled as of Tuesday afternoon: Rep. Mike Thompson was trailing venture capitalist Eric Jones in the 4th District, while Rep. Doris Matsui led Sacramento City Councilmember Mai Vang in the 7th District.

#6117. Is The Amex Gold Card Worth It? 4x Points & $424 In Credits Justify The $325 Fee

The American Express® Gold Card has a $325 annual fee (Rates & Fees), which is obviously on the steep side. While I’ve published a full Amex Gold Card review, in this post I’d like to talk more broadly about whether the Amex Gold Card is worth it, with my firsthand experience.

The Amex Gold Card is an absolute powerhouse for dining purchases, whether you spend money at restaurants or supermarkets, so those are bonus categories that have real value for people. However, when it comes to making the math on the card work, it’s all about how much of the $400+ in annual credits that you can take advantage of, to help offset the fee.

So rather than just summarizing the Amex Gold benefits, I’d like to take a first-person look at how I get value from this card, to account for the points I’m earning and redeeming, and how much of the credits I’m easily able to take advantage of. After all, we shouldn’t judge cards by their published perks, but instead, by our actual use.

Link: Learn more about the American Express® Gold Card

Before getting into individual categories and credits on the Amex Gold Card, here’s where I am on the math over the past year, at the time of this post:

Quite honestly, the math on this card has worked out quite well for me. I don’t want to say I’m coming out ahead on the Amex Gold Card purely in terms of the card’s credits, but they greatly help offset the annual fee, and then the 4x points is what makes the card worthwhile for me. If I could just remember to be a little more consistent with using the dining credits or using the Dunkin’ credits at all, I’d be coming out even further ahead with this product.

The Amex Gold Card has an improved welcome offer where you can earn a bonus as high as 100,000 Membership Rewards points after spending $8,000 within the first six months. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Membership Rewards points to be worth 1.7 cents each. That means to me, those 100,000 points are worth $1,700 (assuming that’s what you’re eligible for).

With a full six months to hit the spending requirement — a little over $1,300 per month — this should be easy enough for many people to complete (and if not, there are always creative ways to complete minimum spending). Thanks to Amex’s “apply with confidence” feature, there won’t be a hard pull unless you accept the offer.

When I applied for the card, the welcome offer was “only” 60,000 points, so this is quite a bit better. I received instant approval on the card. I should also emphasize that the product isn’t available to those who currently have the card, or those who have had the card (or previous versions of the card) in the past.

On top of that, you may not be eligible for the welcome offer on this card if you have or have had American Express Platinum Card® (learn more). That’s why I always recommend applying for the Amex Gold before the Amex Platinum, since that will allow you to eventually earn the welcome offer on both cards. As I see it, you get the Amex Gold for the return on spending, and the Amex Platinum for the perks. In the interest of being thorough, let me also mention that if you have some Chase cards you’re considering applying for, perhaps get those first, given the limitations of the Chase 5/24 rule.

I’ve of course already redeemed a lot of the points earned from the welcome offer on the card, including for a flight in All Nippon Airways first class, which I booked with Air Canada Aeroplan points (moved over from Amex).

This is where the Amex Gold Card really becomes exciting, and where the personal version of the card is nicely differentiated from the business version of the card — the bonus categories are broad, everyday, and hard not to use. The Amex Gold offers:

Based on my valuations, that’s like an 8.5% return on prepaid hotel stays, a 6.8% return at restaurants and at U.S. supermarkets, and a 5.1% return on eligible flights. The 4x points on dining and 4x points on supermarket categories are the two that matter for most people, and they’re genuinely best-in-class.

I’ve just gone over how much spending I’ve put on the card over the past year, and it’s not pretty… yow, food is expensive, especially when you add two little kids to the equation! I’ll simply say that I’ve earned six figures worth of points from the 4x points categories on this card.

I’m not a huge fan of doing math this way, but just to do the breakeven math on the Amex Gold annual fee, based on my valuation of 1.7 cents per Membership Rewards point, spending just under $4,800 per year (just under $400 per month) in the 4x points categories would earn you enough points to help offset the annual fee, not even factoring in any of the other benefits.

I do want to add two caveats to the Amex Gold earning structure, just to balance things:

Eligibility is always determined by how the merchant is categorized, so some places you’d consider a restaurant or grocery store may not code that way, and that’s something to be aware of. It’s certainly an issue I’ve faced a few times with the card, where it didn’t code exactly as I expected.

For example, you typically expect a coffee shop to code as a restaurant for these purposes, but I’ve had a few that didn’t code that way. Fortunately I’m not spending a fortune at coffee shops, so it’s not a huge deal.

Here’s the heart of the “worth it” question, as I see it. The Amex Gold Card offers statement credits that could save you up to $424 per year, more than offsetting the annual fee (Enrollment is required for select benefits).

But they’re fragmented across several buckets, most of them monthly use-it-or-lose-it, so the advertised number and the amount you’re actually able to use can be very different. Here’s how each Amex Gold credit has worked for me, ranked from easiest to hardest to redeem. But first, below is a chart summarizing the basics of the Amex Gold credits (Enrollment is required for select benefits)..

Amex Gold cardmembers receive a $10 Uber Cash credit every calendar month, valid toward Uber and Uber Eats purchases in the United States An Amex Card must be selected as the payment method for your Uber or Uber Eats transaction to redeem the Amex Uber Cash benefit. In order to use this, you need to pay for your purchase with an Amex card, and the Uber Cash can only be deposited in a single account.

This is the Amex Gold credit I maximize most reliably, because it’s effectively cash toward something almost everyone uses — a ride or food delivery. Even if you don’t take Ubers, the credit works on Uber Eats.

Personally, I generally use Lyft for rideshare and Uber Eats for food delivery, so I easily get the full value of this credit each month on food orders alone. I wish I didn’t use Uber Eats so much that I consider it to be “good as cash,” but that’s the current reality.

Amex Gold cardmembers receive a semi-annual Resy credit — a $50 credit in January through June, and a $50 credit in July through December — valid at eligible U.S. Resy restaurants, Resy.com, and in the mobile Resy app. There’s no need to even make a reservation, as long as you pay at an eligible restaurant.

Because it’s semi-annual rather than monthly, it’s lower maintenance, but it requires you to actually dine at a Resy restaurant in each half of the year — which is easy in a major city and harder elsewhere.

As someone who lives in Miami, there’s absolutely no shortage of Resy restaurants, so I get full value out of this with minimal effort. Fortunately whatever part of the meal isn’t covered by the credit still earns 4x points. So over the past year, I’ve gotten the full value out of this… yay! But if you live in a more rural area, you may not have any Resy restaurants near you, and the credit may not be worth much unless you’re traveling.

Amex Gold cardmembers receive a $10 monthly dining credit, for a total of up to $120 each year, valid for purchases with Grubhub (including Seamless), Buffalo Wild Wings, Five Guys, The Cheesecake Factory, and Wonder. Only purchases in the United States qualify, and you’re limited to a single credit no matter how many authorized users you have.

The catch is that it’s tied to a specific list of merchants, so it’s only “easy” if one of those fits your routine. Grubhub is the flexible one for most people.

It goes without saying we all have different spending patterns. Personally, I sort of struggle with the credit. I don’t remember the last time I went to a Buffalo Wild Wings, Five Guys, or The Cheesecake Factory (nothing against them, I sort of love the SkinnyLicious menu, but they’re just not near me), and I don’t even know what Wonder is. So that leaves Grubhub.

I try to use the dining credit on Grubhub whenever I can, but to be honest, many months I forget. That’s because Uber Eats and DoorDash are the primary delivery apps I use. The $10 isn’t necessarily that huge of an incentive to remember, which is why it sometimes slips my mind.

Amex Gold cardmembers receive a $7 monthly Dunkin’ credit, earned after using your enrolled card to pay at more than 9,000 Dunkin’ locations nationwide.

This is the most polarizing credit on the card. If there’s a Dunkin’ on your commute and you actually like Dunkin’, enjoy some coffee on Amex. If there isn’t, you may forfeit $84 of the headline credit total — and it’s worth subtracting from the card’s advertised value when you do your own math. Keep in mind that there aren’t even Dunkin’ locations in some states, like Oregon and Washington.

I have read that a $ 7-per-month reload would trigger the credit as well, so you could accrue it. I probably should’ve been taking advantage of that all along, but this is also where “credit card fatigue” kicks in, and I just forget to even focus on this.

After all, on some level this credit card game is supposed to be fun, rather than just spending every month chasing dozens and dozens of credits. Or maybe I just have too many cards? 😉 So yeah, unfortunately I’ve been losing $84 per year in value with this credit by not taking advantage of it.

Two more perks on the Amex Gold Card are worth a brief mention, because they round out the card without being the reason to get it.

First, Amex Offers. One of the great features of Amex cards is access to Amex Offers, which provides savings or bonus points on purchases with all kinds of retailers. The more Amex cards you have, the more offers you’ll have access to, and they could save you hundreds of dollars per year.

For example, I recently had an Amex Offers deal for 1,200 bonus points when spending $150 with Amazon, and that could be used up to three times. Since I shop on Amazon all the time, that’s an easy bonus of 3,600 points as I see it.

Second, The Hotel Collection. For staying two or more nights at select luxury hotels, you can receive extra benefits through The Hotel Collection, including a $100 hotel credit and a room upgrade if available. This is different than Amex Fine Hotels + Resorts®, which requires having the Amex Platinum. I can’t say that I’ve used this, because when it comes to Amex’s hotel programs, I typically gravitate toward FHR.

Lastly, while I wouldn’t consider it to be particularly valuable either, I should also mention that the Amex Gold offers Hertz Five Star status, which is at least worth being aware of (Enrollment is required for select benefits). This gets you an upgrade to a higher car class on rentals when available as well as a 25% bonus on all Hertz rentals.

The Amex Gold Card has no foreign transaction fees (Rates & Fees), so you can use it for purchases globally — and because the 4x dining category applies at restaurants worldwide, this is genuinely one of the better cards to carry abroad for meals. Just remember the 4x supermarket category is U.S.-only, so that bonus doesn’t follow you overseas.

I use this card all the time for dining abroad, and it’s a good way to maximize rewards. For example, on my summer trip to the Dolomites, I used the Amex Gold Card for all my dining outside hotels, which included some great meals.

I should acknowledge that Amex doesn’t quite have the global acceptance of Mastercard or Visa, for example, though the gap is much smaller than in the past.

I think the Amex Gold Card is a product that has bonus categories that are about as well rounded as one could imagine, in terms of appealing to the average consumer. Everyone eats, and this card is great for those people, whether you get your food at restaurants or supermarkets.

I will say, the math on this card may break down for you if you fall into one of the following two categories:

Personally, the math on this card is working great for me. I do wish I more consistently maximized the credits, as I do a pretty good job, but not a great job. Based on my own usage patterns, I basically view this as a card costing me well under $100 per year (after subtracting the value of the credits), and then I get a very well balanced return in some bonus categories for that. I guess I just need to do a better job of actually using those Dunkin’ credits, and at least reloading my account.

I also think it’s worth emphasizing that the Amex Gold might not be the right style of card for some people, depending on your consumer preferences:

For me, the Amex Gold Card is proving to be a keeper, and I plan to renew on my account anniversary, while paying the annual fee. The rewards structure on this card is excellent and simple, while the credits help make this an affordable card to hold onto. So if you ask me, the card is a clear “yes” if:

If you’d forfeit two or more of the credits, do the math on the credits you’ll actually take advantage of before counting the full $424 — the card can still win on dining and supermarket earning alone, but the real math is different than the marketed amount.

The other nice thing is that if you get the Amex Gold and decide after a year or more that the card is no longer a good fit for you, you can typically product change it to another card. This allows you to preserve the rewards, credit history, etc.

The Amex Gold Card is one of American Express’ best rewards cards for earning points, with 4x points on dining and U.S. supermarkets, which is hard for any other card to beat. The earning side is the easy part — almost everyone can use it.

Whether the card is worth its $325 annual fee on an ongoing basis comes down to one honest question: how many of the up to $424 in annual credits will you actually capture? The credit is real — up to $120 for dining, up to $120 in Uber Cash, up to $100 with Resy, and up to $84 with Dunkin’ — but it’s fragmented, and the gap between the headline and your real capture rate is the whole decision.

It’s easiest to make the math work if you actually spend a substantial amount on the 4x points categories, since the value of that will quickly make a material difference to your points earning.

What’s your take on the value proposition of the Amex Gold Card? Which credits do you actually capture each year, and which ones do you forfeit?

#6115. Jim Jordan picked as new minority leader for House GOP

House Republicans on Tuesday opted for a new face atop their ranks, electing Rep. Jim Jordan as the incoming minority leader for the 120th Congress after Republicans suffered massive losses in last week’s midterm elections.

The Ohio Republican defeated outgoing Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., in a closed-door, secret-ballot election. The final tally was 106-73.

“Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families. Democrats offer more government. We will offer more freedom,” Jordan said after the hourslong process.

The two had been working the phones before making their pitches during a candidates forum in the Capitol Visitor Center’s auditorium on Tuesday morning. Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., announced last week he would not seek a leadership post in the new Congress, which will be seated on Jan. 3.

“Obviously Jim and I know each other, but I’ve got a proven record of how to bring people together,” Scalise said ahead of the vote, trying to play up his experience, including more than a decade on the leadership team that included a stint as whip.

As House Republicans trickled out of the candidates’ forum for breaks or to take phone calls, one member, granted anonymity to discuss a private session, said Scalise and Jordan “both have strong points, but they both have flaws.” Each made an unsuccessful bid for speaker in 2023 after the ouster of Kevin McCarthy, before the gavel ultimately went to Johnson.

Declining to reveal which would get his vote, the member said: “I won’t talk about a secret vote, but I know who I think is best to lead us.”

The incoming minority conference also selected other leaders on Tuesday.

Majority Whip Tom Emmer of Minnesota held off a challenge from Texas Rep. August Pfluger to become minority whip in January, despite some grumbling about how tight votes were handled on the floor this year.

“We’ve got to retool our whip operation,” Texas Rep. Nathaniel Moran said Tuesday morning, pointing to “the number of times we were held up by either discharge petitions or failed rule votes.”

“Those were things that should not have happened in the majority,” said Moran as he publicly backed Pfluger for whip.

But Emmer projected confidence after his whip win, comparing the moment to when Republicans were down and out after their losses in 2018 only to rebound a few years later.

“To our colleagues on the left, enjoy this honeymoon phase, because come Jan. 3, 2027, you will regret ever putting your name on a ballot,” he said at a news conference, adding that Republicans under his watch would expose the “empty promises” that Democrats made to voters and push back on what he called their “radical” agenda.

In the day’s only three-way race, conference Chair Lisa McClain of Michigan defeated Reps. Erin Houchin of Indiana and Greg Steube of Florida to keep her spot.

“We had a spirited leadership election. There were important conversations about the future of our conference, and I listened,” McClain said at the news conference.

In the race to lead House Republicans’ campaign arm, Rep. Brian Jack of Georgia defeated Rep. Rudy Yakym of Indiana, seen as an up-and-coming Ways and Means Committee member. That means Jack will take on a huge share of the uphill task of selecting candidates and raising funds for the 2028 cycle as he helms the National Republican Congressional Committee.

But most of the attention heading into Tuesday’s closed-door proceedings was on the minority leader race.

Johnson, the outgoing speaker, declined to endorse a candidate but had encouraging words for Jordan after his win. “He’s going to do an excellent job. He’s a good, trusted friend and brother,” he said.

Rep. Tom Cole, R-Okla., said it was a “tough choice for the conference to make,” but he wasn’t disappointed in the pick. “He was an exceptionally capable chairman of both Oversight and Judiciary. He’s excellent in an interview,” Cole said of Jordan. “He’s got boundless energy and determination.”

Jordan’s victory means he will form a political and legal tag team with newly installed White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller in pushing back on a number of investigations House Democrats have planned for President Donald Trump, some of his second-term administration officials and his business-minded family members.

Democrats will have more than 250 seats in the chamber, with a number of races still uncalled. Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, expected to become the next House speaker, told reporters last week he predicts Democrats will have at least 255 seats when all the ballots have been counted and verification processes have played out.

“It’s a historic majority in the 21st century,” Jeffries told reporters in Washington, D.C., the day after the midterms. “The American people have chosen the economy over extremism. The American people have chosen hope over hatred. The American people have chosen common sense over corruption, chaos and cruelty. The American people have chosen House Democrats because they want to see a dramatic change in direction.”

Political analysts have predicted an internal battle within the GOP for the direction the party takes over the next two years — and after Trump leaves office in January 2029.

The Institute for Legislative Analysis, a nonprofit organization that advocates to shrink the size and influence of the government, released a vote study assessment on Monday. Its calculations led ILA to endorse Emmer and three fresh faces: Jordan, Steube and Jack.

“It’s clear many Republican voters feel their representatives in Washington aren’t representing them,” Ryan McGowan, the institute’s CEO, said in a statement. “It will be interesting to see whether House Republicans respond by choosing leaders … whose voting records are much more closely aligned with the party’s conservative base.”

Several GOP sources late last week, granted anonymity to be candid, said they were expecting a close outcome between Scalise and Jordan, adding Emmer was working the phones hard to remain whip. One said having either Scalise or Jordan atop the conference, with the expectation of Emmer staying on as whip, “won’t be much of a change at the top.”

The new leadership team will take over Jan. 3, when Democrats are expected to, in part, use their large majority to target all things Trump 2.0. The same GOP source said the majority party will “inevitably be pursuing impeachment by August recess despite their disciplined statements to the media pre-election.”

Trump replied in the affirmative when a “60 Minutes” correspondent asked him in an interview that aired Sunday night if he could work with Democrats, should they also be aggressively investigating his team.

“Well, I did it for four years,” the president said of his first term. “They impeached me twice. And there are those that say that worked out to my advantage.”

Nina Heller, Michael Macagnone and Samantha Freeman contributed to this report.

#6114. Allegiant, Sun Country Add New Destinations, 16 Routes

Allegiant and Sun Country are adding new destinations and a combined 16 routes ahead of the summer of 2027.

Allegiant said Tuesday that it will resume service to Minneapolis, while Sun Country will expand to Belleville, Illinois (via MidAmerica St. Louis Airport), Gulf Shores, Alabama, and Knoxville, Tennessee.

Notably, Minneapolis is Sun Country’s main operating base; renewed service from Allegiant is expected to bring their networks closer together.

Allegiant acquired Sun Country in May, though for the time being they are continuing to operate as separate airlines.

“Minnesota is an essential part of the future of our combined company, and today’s announcement is another step in delivering on that commitment,” Allegiant CEO Greg Anderson said in a news release. “MSP is our largest base of operations by a wide margin, and we see opportunities for continued growth there. Combining Sun Country’s strong foundation in the Twin Cities with Allegiant’s nationwide network of communities will provide Minnesota travelers with more convenient, affordable nonstop travel options.”

The new routes will come online in April and May.

Additionally, Allegiant said it will operate four routes currently flown by Sun Country:

Allegiant and Sun Country are expected to eventually merge operations, with the Sun Country brand phased out, though it is not clear exactly when this will happen. Allegiant said Tuesday that it will continue operating separately from Sun Country “until 2028 or later.”

#6113. United Airlines Cancels 7 Routes From 3rd Busiest Hub: See Full List Now

United Airlines is the world's third-largest airline for flights and seats for sale. However, due to the Star Alliance member's strong long-haul operation — it has more long-haul flights than any other operator — it ranks first globally for available seat miles.

United has seven hubs in the mainland US: Chicago O'Hare, Denver, Houston Intercontinental, Los Angeles, Newark, San Francisco, and Washington Dulles. With 948 daily movements, influenced by much regional jet activity, OAG data shows that Houston Intercontinental has the third-highest number of departures.

United's schedule from Houston for January 2026 to March 2027 has been compared to what is planned to operate from next April. This process shows that eight routes have ended or will cease soon, two of which are international. No future flights are scheduled, but this could change. It reflects what is known as of November 17.

All the airline's routes to Tulum are ending. US Department of Transportation (DOT) data shows that Houston had an overall load factor through August 2026 of just 65.6%. No wonder it is ending

The link to Vancouver was served on a year-round basis, often with a double daily operation in the summer and no more than a daily flight in the winter. As no services are scheduled beyond April next year, it is reasonable to assume that it is ending. The 737-800 and 737-900 will be deployed in the remaining months.

Fellow Star Alliance member Air Canada runs daily. The 137-seat A220-300 will operate this winter, with the 196-seat A321 next summer. Perhaps reflecting the absence of United, that'll be the airline's highest-capacity equipment to date.

As part of the announcement, Allegiant will pull out of Chicago Midway. Find out more now!

Flights in what were three brand-new markets do not appear to be returning. Service to Portland, Maine, materialized in June last year, followed by Burlington, Vermont, and Spokane, Washington, in May 2026. In all cases, no nonstop service is scheduled next summer. They only had a Saturday-only operation.

Burlington exclusively saw Mesa's 76-seat Embraer E175s, while Spokane was in the hands of SkyWest's E175s. Portland was a bit different, as mainline A319s coexisted with Mesa E175s. The three routes were United Express's three longest regional jet links from Houston Intercontinental in 2026. At 1,473 nautical miles (2,728 km), Houston-Spokane was the carrier's second-longest RJ route network-wide, after San Francisco-St. Louis.

Covering 1,329 nautical miles (2,461 km), the link from Texas's second-busiest airport to Nevada's second-busiest airport has been served for many years. DOT data shows that Continental inaugurated flights in 1993, but it is possible that they existed before then. They returned in 1998 and operated until 2008, influenced by the Global Financial Crisis. Service resumed in 2011.

In the 12 months to August 2026, DOT data shows that only 10,667 round-trip passengers were transported. That tiny volume was because flights usually only existed on weekends. The load factor was 81.6%, with most passengers (58.1%) only flying between Houston and Reno. It appears that the final departure is set for February 27 on the A319. However, while the route is usually served on a year-round basis, it is possible, but unconfirmed, that it'll become winter-seasonal and return next winter.

#6112. Transfer Capital One Miles To Qatar Airways Privilege Club With 15% Bonus: Worth It?

The Capital One mileage program has just introduced a new bonus for points transfers to Qatar Airways Privilege Club. While the percentage bonus amount isn’t huge, there’s potentially value to be had, especially given the flexibility these rewards offer.

Between November 15 and December 14, 2026, it’s possible to receive a 15% bonus when moving points from Capital One to Qatar Airways Privilege Club. This is being offered on Capital One’s end, so when you go the mileage transfer page, make sure that you see this offer available.

Ordinarily rewards transfer between programs at a 1:1 ratio (in increments of 1,000 miles), while through this promotion you’d get 1,150 Qatar Airways Privilege Club Avios for every 1,000 Capital One miles transferred. Points transfers from Capital One to Qatar Airways are typically instant, and the bonus rewards will post the same time as the standard rewards.

We see transferable points currencies frequently offer bonuses on transfers to a variety of Avios currencies, and you can of course move rewards between those various currencies. We’ve definitely seen bigger than 15% bonuses in the past, but there’s no guarantee we’ll see a higher offer return anytime soon.

I’d argue that the Qatar Airways Privilege Club program is pretty lucrative nowadays. For one, keep in mind that Qatar Airways uses Avios as its rewards currency, so it’s possible to transfer Avios at a 1:1 ratio between the various programs that earn Avios. That includes Aer Lingus AerClub, British Airways Club, Finnair Plus, and Iberia Plus.

This means that you could use this offer to indirectly convert Citi ThankYou points into British Airways Avios with a 15% bonus as well. That’s something that will no doubt interest some.

However, there’s also huge value directly with the Qatar Airways Privilege Club program. Privilege Club has decent award pricing on Qatar Airways flights, and also has access to more business class award availability than partner programs (though availability still isn’t great). Privilege Club also has several unique airline partners, ranging from JetBlue, to RwandAir, to Virgin Australia, opening up valuable redemption opportunities.

Through December 14, 2026, the Capital One program is offering a 15% bonus on points transfers to Qatar Airways Privilege Club. If you’re looking to acquire any “flavor” of Avios, this could be a great value, as this is also a way to get rewards with British Airways, Iberia, etc.

However, if you’re thinking of making a speculative transfer to earn Avios, I might wait for a bigger offer, as we do sometimes see 30%+ bonuses on transfers to some Avios currencies.
