#6111. Rep. Darren Soto survives Republican-drawn map in Florida

Florida Rep. Darren Soto, the most vulnerable House Democrat running for reelection, narrowly won a sixth term Tuesday in a district that state Republicans redrew in their favor.

Soto was leading Republican Navy veteran Dan Green by less than a point when The Associated Press called the race for Central Florida’s 9th District a week after Election Day. His margin of victory was above the 0.5 percent threshold that would trigger a recount under state law.

House Democrats have so far flipped more than 40 seats and appear on track to hold their biggest majority in the chamber in decades. Soto’s win means that no House Democratic incumbent lost to a Republican in the general election this year. And Florida Democrats defended all four seats the GOP had hoped to pick up under the state’s new Republican-drawn map.

Democratic Reps. Kathy Castor and Jared Moskowitz both won reelection from districts that shifted red, while Democrat Pia Dandiya, a former high school principal, defeated Republican Marine Corps veteran Casey Askar for a redrawn open seat in South Florida.

Soto, who declared victory last week, had been seen as the most vulnerable of the targeted Florida Democrats. The new map reduced the Hispanic population of his district as the seat shifted from one that Kamala Harris would have carried in 2024 to one that Donald Trump would have taken by 18 points.

“Despite the Florida Republican legislature’s efforts to redraw me out of this district, my record of delivering for Florida showed voters that I am a reliable fighter for them in Congress,” Soto said in a Nov. 4 statement.

In a Tuesday memo detailing how House Democrats secured their historic majority, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee took aim at Republicans’ mid-decade redistricting efforts, saying their “attempts to steal seats … supremely backfired.”

While Florida Republicans were unsuccessful in flipping the four Democrat-held seats, the party held all of its House seats in the Sunshine State. Republican Rep. María Elvira Salazar narrowly won reelection in the Miami-area 27th District over Democratic challenger Eliott Rodriguez, the AP reported Tuesday. In the 7th District outside Orlando, Republican former TV news anchor Ryan Elijah defeated Democratic Navy veteran Bale Dalton, a former NASA chief of staff who conceded Tuesday.

Delta Air Lines and Hyatt have announced the much-anticipated details of their new loyalty partnership.

The new arrangement will allow certain SkyMiles and World of Hyatt members to “double dip” their earnings on flights and hotel stays.

That means you could earn both Delta miles and Hyatt points on a flight — or a hotel booking. The setup is reminiscent of what Hyatt previously shared with American Airlines.

However, there are two big rules to know about this Delta-Hyatt arrangement:

For Delta Medallion and World of Hyatt elite members, this partnership will open up more ways to earn points and miles.

Plus, the partnership includes new loyalty perks that members can unlock as they climb the status ladder.

For instance, Delta will add Hyatt free-night certificates to its menu of choice benefits available at the Platinum and Diamond Medallion levels.

Hyatt elites can opt for Delta benefits like e-certificates and Sky Club passes as they reach certain milestones.

Let's get to the details of how to link your account, and how the earnings will work.

To start earning SkyMiles on Hyatt stays and World of Hyatt points on Delta flights, you’ll need to link your two loyalty accounts.

You can do that through this page on Delta’s website or this one via Hyatt’s.

You’ll start earning right away on eligible flights and hotel stays.

There are bonus points on the table for members who act quickly.

All members can earn those bonus points, whether they have elite status or not.

Even sooner, though, members who link their World of Hyatt and Delta SkyMiles accounts can register to earn one additional elite night credit on their first qualifying stay completed between Nov. 17 and Dec. 31, 2026. Eligible stays are those booked as paid or award nights.

Delta flyers who earn Medallion elite status will be eligible to earn SkyMiles on eligible Hyatt bookings.

Medallions will earn 1 mile per $1 of eligible spend at participating Hyatt properties.

You’ll earn those Delta miles on top of the standard points (and elite night credits) that you’d earn as a World of Hyatt member.

Similarly, World of Hyatt elite members can earn points on Delta flights.

That’s on top of the Delta miles (and Medallion Qualifying Dollars) you’d earn for your booking.

While Delta’s coach fares are not eligible for World of Hyatt earnings, you can still earn Hyatt points on the carrier’s basic premium fares like Comfort Basic, Basic business, etc.

This new partnership between Delta SkyMiles and World of Hyatt certainly unlocks more earning opportunities for loyalty members across both programs.

The setup is clearly tilted heavily toward travelers who have status — and those who are willing to pay more for a premium ticket. You have to be “elite” to take full advantage of the tie-up, and can’t earn Hyatt points on a regular Delta main cabin booking.

However, travelers who are already committed Delta and Hyatt loyalists will come out ahead, gaining the ability to stack their earnings on both flights and hotel stays.

The SkyMiles-World of Hyatt partnership also includes a host of new benefits that members of both programs can select as they earn higher status.

Those options will go live on Feb. 1, when Delta starts its new Medallion qualification year.

Before opting for a free night award, you'll obviously want to weigh that perk against the other options you have, which range from Sky Club memberships to travel vouchers on Delta.

Hyatt is also layering in Delta benefits to its menu of Milestone Rewards, which members can select upon hitting certain elite thresholds.

#6109. Alaska Cuts Four Routes

Alaska Airlines will drop four destinations from its network in Portland, Oregon.

The carrier confirmed it will end service from Portland to Baltimore, St. Louis, New Orleans, and Jackson Hole, Wyoming.

Three of the connections launched only months ago. Portland-Jackson Hole came online in June, and service to Baltimore and St. Louis started in May.

“As we add new routes to our network, we constantly assess existing routes to ensure we’re using our aircraft in the markets our guests want most,” the carrier said in a statement provided to AirlineGeeks. “As part of that process, we’ve made the decision to discontinue service between Portland and Baltimore, Jackson Hole, St. Louis, and New Orleans. We remain committed to Portland and will continue to invest in opportunities that strengthen our network there, including adding service in markets where we see the greatest opportunities for our guests.”

Alaska serves over 60 destinations from Portland, and recently opened a new lounge there.

#6108. Hello, OMAAT Readers! How I Got Here And What’s Next

Isn’t this a little surreal? After years of reading OMAAT, here I am writing my very first post.

First of all, a huge thank you to Ben for such a lovely introduction, and for everyone who gave me such a warm welcome in the comments already. I’m really looking forward to getting to know the OMAAT community Ben has built over the years.

In the first of what will undoubtedly be a lot of posts for One Mile at a Time, I thought I’d share a bit about who I am and what you can expect from me going forward.

I’m literally asking myself that as I write this.

Funnily enough, it was never my dream to be a writer, journalist, blogger, or anything similar. The only thing I can ever remember wanting to be “when I grew up” was a pilot. Despite several applications and reaching the final stage of cadet schemes with Aer Lingus and British Airways, it didn’t work out for me.

Determined to work in the industry, I quit my soul-destroying city job in London to do a Master’s in Air Transport Management at the University of Loughborough in the U.K. I was then offered 2 very different jobs: a junior marketing role with Air Transat, or to be part of a small team starting up TPG’s U.K. office. As a natural risk-taker, I took the latter. After almost 8 years of writing for various publications and dabbling in some video content, I’ve realized that this is what I was meant to be doing all along — the job just didn’t exist when I wanted to be a pilot as a kid.

So why OMAAT? Why now? I spent the last 2 years traveling the world, working remotely, in search of somewhere I felt connected enough to call home. In my heart of hearts, I always knew that was going to be Rio, so I moved here in September this year. I’ve also been considering a more permanent home for my writing and my online presence, so when happenstance did its thing and Ben offered me a full-time online home at OMAAT, it was the perfect opportunity.

I’m honored to have been entrusted to write alongside Ben, whose expertise I’ve learned from over the years. While I don’t promise to be an expert on everything, my almost 8 years of experience in this industry should hopefully mean my expertise meets the standard expected here.

What started out as a passion for planes and aviation has turned into a love of all things travel, loyalty, and the miles and points that help make it happen. I’m really looking forward to sharing some of my learnings, experiences, and tips and tricks from the past couple of years that should complement Ben’s breadth of knowledge.

To start with, much of what you’ll see from me will be written. But as Ben said, the plan is to gradually bring in more video and social content, which I’m really looking forward to helping OMAAT with.

I’m also a self-proclaimed expert on Rio and Brazil (I’ve been coming here since 2009), so if there’s any specific Rio, Brazil, or wider South American travel advice, reviews, or insights you’d like, I’d be more than happy to help, even if it means I have to hop a plane for the research. 😝

I’ll leave it at that for now, as I need to get packing to fly across the Pond for an exciting aviation event this week. All will be revealed soon. 🤓✈️

I’m very excited and honored to be Ben’s first full-time writer in a very long time. Today is the first day of a new adventure for myself, Ben, and the OMAAT behind-the-scenes team, and I can’t wait to bring you, the readers, along for the ride.

#6107. Thune will lead Republicans through the minority

Senate Majority Leader John Thune was reelected as the Republican leader on Tuesday and will steer the conference through their time in the minority.

The South Dakotan ran uncontested despite a push from some of his colleagues to delay the leadership elections following Republicans’ stunning defeats last week in the midterms, which saw them lose at least seven seats and the majority.

“Obviously, the election result was not what we hoped for,” Thune told reporters, referring to the midterms. “But I think it’s important that we take the lessons from that and internalize the message the American people were sending to us.”

While he and the rest of the leadership slate sailed through the conference contests by voice vote, it wasn’t without drama.

Before the leadership elections began in the Old Supreme Court Chamber early Tuesday morning, the conference held a meeting at the request of a group of GOP five senators, led by Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis.

The conversation, which several senators described as “frank,” ended up pushing back the leadership elections by a few hours. But they were not postponed to another day as some had hoped.

“This has never been anything against John Thune,” said Johnson, as he made good on his commitment to leave the room early if the conference proceeded with its election. “What I didn’t agree with was holding the election right away, giving nobody an opportunity to really challenge any leadership position.”

“Part of the issue here is who wants the job? God bless him for serving,” Johnson added.

The conference conversation Tuesday morning turned into an “open-mic” with both conservatives and those who lost their elections speaking, according to senators.

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., told reporters, “To rush into this and to just ratify all the same leadership — I mean, what message does that send?”

But no contender to Thune emerged despite the angst, and a motion to proceed to the election, introduced by Thune’s fellow South Dakotan Sen. Mike Rounds, was accepted.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said voters who rejected Republicans last week were reacting to high gas prices, the war in Iran and the cost of living, not to how Senate leaders were running the conference.

“I don’t think anybody in Texas who voted for the Democrat governor was voting against John Thune. If you diagnose that as a problem, you’re misdiagnosing the problem,” Paul said.

Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo., was reelected to his position, as was the chairman of the Senate Republican Conference, Tom Cotton of Arkansas. Sen. James Lankford of Oklahoma was again selected as vice chair of the conference, while Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia was reelected as Republican Policy Committee chair.

“Our first step is to make sure the American people know that we heard what they said, and the American people’s priorities are our priorities. That’s the way we regain their trust,” Barrasso said afterward.

Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio got the nod to chair the National Republican Senatorial Committee, meaning he will helm the campaign arm as the party looks ahead to the uncertain waters of 2028.

Moreno said, “I was in the retail automobile business, so when you don’t listen to your customers, your customers punish you. I think we have to own it, and I think we have to learn from it.”

Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., said on Monday evening, “What we as a conference right now need is honesty. We need focus. We need to try to reach a consensus on what we need to change.”

Kennedy was among those pushing to delay the leadership elections and told reporters on Tuesday he voted present instead of yes on whether to proceed to them.

Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., who ran for GOP leader twice — once in 2022 against Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., and in 2024 against Thune — declined to run again to challenge Thune. But in a Dear Colleague letter on Monday, he detailed what he’d like to see in the lame-duck session before Democrats take power, including confirming every nominee President Donald Trump has sent to the Senate, funding the government without an omnibus, banning stock trading, passing the permitting bill that is advancing this week in the Senate, passing the National Defense Authorization Act, balancing the budget and pushing through a sweeping voter ID bill known as the SAVE America Act.

Senate Republicans on Tuesday also voted on a resolution on their path forward that was spurred by a motion from Scott, aides said.

“It is the sense of the GOP Conference that we will maximize the 54 days we have with congressional majorities, to confirm every judicial nominee and every executive nominee that the conference approves of, to pass our core Republican priorities, and to do everything humanly possible to pass a reconciliation bill before Jan. 3,” the resolution reads in part.

That long list of goals highlights the expectations Thune has faced as leader, where he led one-third of Republicans’ trifecta in Washington. In the next Congress, Democrats will hold the majority in both chambers of Congress after their larger-than-expected wins, while Trump finishes out his term as president.

Thune said he told his conference: “As I look back on the last couple of years, my question is, what would you have me do differently?”

“Given the constraints we had to deal with, all the stuff that was coming at us on a daily basis, a narrow margin in the House, the White House, the Democrats over here who were obstructing two long government shutdowns — I think we came out of it as well as could have been expected, and got a lot of stuff done,” Thune told reporters.

“If you believe the exit polls, it was the war, it was the economy, it was inflation, it was fuel prices,” Thune added. “So no, I wasn’t apologizing for anything that we did. And I think on the political side, I don’t know what else I could have done.”

#6106. 5 Injured After 'Severe Turbulence' Hits Fort Lauderdale-Bound JetBlue A320

A JetBlue Airbus A320 carrying passengers from Puerto Rico to Florida encountered severe turbulence on November 17, 2026, leaving five people reporting injuries or requiring medical evaluation. Flight 1717, traveling from Ponce Mercedita International Airport (PSE) to Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport (FLL), landed safely at approximately 06:58 local time, where emergency personnel were waiting to assist those affected.

The incident involved both passengers and crew members, prompting a response from Broward Sheriff Fire Rescue shortly before the aircraft's arrival. Although five people required medical attention, none were transported to the hospital, and authorities reported no structural damage to the aircraft. The incident is another reminder of the risks turbulence continues to pose to airline passengers and cabin crew, even when flights land safely.

JetBlue Flight 1717 was operating between Puerto Rico and Fort Lauderdale earlier today when it encountered severe turbulence. According to AeroInside's aviation incident report, the aircraft was an Airbus A320-200 registered as N524JB. The turbulence reportedly injured several people on board, including passengers and cabin crew members.

Broward Sheriff Fire Rescue received reports of multiple injuries at approximately 06:25 local time, according to information provided to local media. The aircraft subsequently landed safely at approximately 06:58 and proceeded to Terminal 3, where emergency personnel were standing by to assess those affected. Fire rescue officials identified five individuals who either reported injuries or required medical evaluation. All five declined transportation to nearby hospitals, and no patients were taken away from the airport.

JetBlue also confirmed the incident in a statement, explaining that medical personnel assessed passengers and crew members after landing.

"JetBlue flight 1717 from Ponce, Puerto Rico (PSE), to Fort Lauderdale (FLL) experienced turbulence during the flight. The aircraft landed safely, where medical personnel evaluated customers and crewmembers for injuries. No one was transported to a hospital. The safety of our customers and crewmembers remains our top priority."

Although turbulence is routine in commercial aviation, severe encounters can cause serious injuries, especially when passengers or crew members are not securely seated. Sudden changes in an aircraft's movement can throw people against cabin structures, while unsecured service equipment and personal belongings can become dangerous projectiles. Flight attendants are particularly exposed because their duties frequently require them to move around the cabin during flight.

The circumstances surrounding JetBlue's encounter have not been fully established. However, CNN Weather reported that thunderstorms were affecting the Turks and Caicos Islands and the southern Bahamas on Tuesday morning. Storm systems were reportedly reaching altitudes of up to 46,000 feet (14,021 meters), potentially requiring aircraft operating in the region to navigate around particularly intense weather. Other aircraft in the area had also reported light to moderate turbulence.

Importantly, turbulence does not necessarily lead to an aircraft malfunction or structural problem. Modern airliners are designed to withstand substantial aerodynamic forces, and an aircraft can remain structurally sound despite a particularly uncomfortable encounter. In this case, authorities confirmed there were no reports of structural damage after Flight 1717's arrival.

A midair plummet leaves three hospitalized.

The JetBlue incident follows another serious turbulence-related event involving an Airbus A320 in October 2026. On October 9, an Avianca flight traveling from Medellín, Colombia, to New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) encountered severe turbulence and diverted to Miami International Airport (MIA). Nine people were injured, including six passengers and three crew members, with several requiring hospital treatment. One individual was reportedly taken to a trauma center with serious injuries.

Another significant incident occurred in May 2026, when a Cathay Pacific Airbus A350-900 operating Flight CX156 from Brisbane (BNE) to Hong Kong (HKG) encountered severe turbulence approximately two hours before landing. Ten people were injured, including six cabin crew members and four passengers. Reports described a sudden aircraft drop that reportedly caught passengers during the meal service, highlighting the potential consequences of unexpected turbulence when people are moving around the cabin.

These incidents underline why airlines and aviation authorities continue to emphasize keeping seat belts fastened whenever passengers are seated, even when the seat belt sign has been switched off. While pilots can use weather forecasts, onboard radar and reports from other aircraft to identify potentially turbulent conditions, clear-air turbulence can be particularly difficult to anticipate visually. For JetBlue, Flight 1717's safe arrival meant the incident ended without hospital transportation or reported aircraft damage, although the five reported injuries show that even a relatively short encounter can affect those on board.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

This is why wise customers keep their seatbelts fastened at all times.

#6105. Delta Reserve Credit Card Review: Benefits Worth It For Delta Loyalists?

American Express and Delta have had a close relationship for many years. As part of that, they issue seven co-branded Delta Amex cards. The Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card is the most premium of these cards, and in this post, I’d like to take an in-depth look at the product. The Delta Reserve Card is worth it if you’re a frequent flyer with Delta, or if you want to earn elite status through credit card spending. Let’s take a look at all the details of the card.

Link: Learn more about the Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card

Before I get into my Delta Reserve Card review, here are some of the card’s key details, from its current welcome bonus to its annual fee and the perks you get with Delta:

I also put together my list of top pros and cons for the Delta Reserve Card:

Let’s look at the Delta Reserve Card‘s welcome bonus offer, eligibility rules, and fees. All of these are probably top of mind if you’re considering applying for this card.

The Delta Reserve Card currently has the following welcome offer: You may be eligible for as high as 125,000 Bonus Miles after you spend $5,000 in eligible purchases on your new Card in your first 6 months of Card Membership. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Delta SkyMiles to be worth 1.1 cents each. That means to me, the 125,000-mile bonus is worth $1,375. While Delta SkyMiles is far from my favorite mileage currency, it does have quite a high floor value, so there are good ways to redeem Delta SkyMiles.

The welcome bonus offer on the Delta Reserve Card is “once in a lifetime,” so it’s not available to you if you currently have the card, or if you’ve had the card in the past. However, eligibility for the Delta Reserve Card (including the welcome offer) is unrelated to whether you have any other personal card in the portfolio. You’re also eligible for the personal card if you already have the business card, and vice versa.

You can read more about Amex’s general application restrictions here.

The Delta Reserve Card has a $650 annual fee (Rates & Fees). Obviously that’s on the high side, though you also get quite a few perks. You can add authorized users for $175 each, and authorized users get some card benefits, including airport lounge access and inflight savings on Delta.

If you spend on the Delta Reserve Card, the good news is that there are no foreign transaction fees (Rates & Fees), so you can efficiently use the card abroad.

Beyond the welcome bonus, how does the Delta Reserve Card earn rewards on your spending, both in terms of miles earned and in terms of elite status qualification? Let’s look at the ongoing earning rates and Medallion Qualification Dollars (MQDs) you can earn through spending on the card.

The Delta Reserve Card has fairly limited bonus categories for spending. The Delta Reserve Card earns:

Ironically, other Delta cards with lower annual fees have more robust bonus categories. The logic is probably that this is the most rewarding card for spending counting toward elite status, and therefore Delta believes that’s enough of an incentive.

Nowadays, Delta SkyMiles Medallion elite status is earned exclusively based on how many Medallion Qualification Dollars (MQDs) you rack up. When it comes to earning MQDs through credit card spending, the Delta Reserve Credit Card is as good as it gets:

For context, Delta SkyMiles Medallion elite status has the following annual MQD requirements:

Therefore if you wanted to earn elite status exclusively through credit card spending, you’d need to spend the following amounts:

While Delta SkyMiles is far from my favorite mileage currency, it does have a high floor value, so there are good ways to redeem Delta SkyMiles.

Delta One (business class) awards can be a great option, especially on roundtrip awards rather than one way itineraries. Using SkyMiles for shorter hops on Delta can be great, too. I’ve seen award flights between New York (LGA) and Orlando (MCO) for less than 20,000 miles roundtrip.

Partner award flights can be an especially good option if you focus on flights that don’t touch the United States, since flights that do are more expensive and get you less value for your miles.

You can redeem SkyMiles for flights on SkyTeam partners, like Air France, China Airlines, and Korean Air. You can also redeem SkyMiles on some airlines that aren’t part of SkyTeam but still partner with Delta, like LATAM and WestJet.

One of the primary things that sets the Delta Reserve Credit Card apart from other Delta Amex cards is the lounge access perks that it offers. The card offers Delta Sky Club® access, Centurion Lounge access, and even several Sky Club passes. How does that work?

The Delta Reserve Card offers 15 Delta Sky Club visits each Medallion year for the primary cardmember. Each visit is defined as all entries within a 24-hour period, including at different airports. In other words, if you have a connecting itinerary, you can visit multiple Sky Clubs at different airports while using only one visit allotment.

It’s possible to unlock unlimited Sky Club visits after spending $75,000 in purchases on your card in a calendar year. Once all 15 visits have been used, eligible cardmembers may purchase additional Sky Club visits at a per visit rate of $50 per person using the card.

In addition to the primary cardmember getting Sky Club access when flying Delta the same day, they also receive four Sky Club guest passes annually.

These can be used by the primary cardmember to guest others into the lounge, allowing you to skip the $50 guesting fee four times annually.

The Delta Reserve Card also offers complimentary Centurion Lounge access when traveling on a same-day Delta flight booked with the card. The primary cardmember is entitled to access, and bringing additional guests costs $50 each.

Centurion Lounges, for the most part, offer a significantly improved food and beverage offering compared to most domestic airline lounges in the United States, so this is a nice option to have.

The Delta Reserve Credit Card has a good bonus, though if I were just looking for the best welcome bonus offer, I would go for the Gold or Platinum version of the card, since the cards have significantly lower annual fees.

The reason you want to get the Reserve version of the card is because of the valuable long term perks that it offers. Above I’ve talked about how the Reserve Card can help you earn status and can help you access lounges, though there are lots of perks beyond that. Let’s take a look at some of those benefits.

Every year upon renewal of the Delta Reserve Card, you receive a roundtrip companion certificate valid within the United States (including Alaska and Hawaii), and to Mexico, the Caribbean, and Central America. This can be used for fares ranging from first class to economy, so the flexibility offered by that is pretty awesome, and for many will more than justify the annual fee.

You just have to pay the government-imposed taxes and fees for the companion. There are some things to be aware of when redeeming the Delta companion certificate, including:

Just for having the Delta Reserve Card, you receive a $200 Delta Stays credit annually. The way this works, you receive up to $200 in statement credits per calendar year when you use your card to pay for a new Delta Stays prepaid hotel or vacation rental booking on the Delta Stays platform.

While I’m not usually a fan of using airline portals to book hotel stays and vacation rentals, this could prove worthwhile, as you can use it for a hotel stay costing right around $200, if you wanted to. If used right, the value here is considerable.

Just for having the Delta Reserve Card, you receive up to $240 in Resy credits annually (Enrollment required). The way this works, you can receive up to $20 in statement credits each month after using your card on eligible purchases at U.S. restaurants that offer reservations on Resy.com and the Resy app, purchases made directly on Resy.com or in the Resy app, and purchases made via Resy Pay.

Just for having the Delta Reserve Card, you receive up to $120 in rideshare credits annually (Enrollment required). The way this works, you can receive up to $10 in statement credits each month after using your card on U.S. rideshare purchases with select providers, including Uber and Lyft.

Just for having the Delta Reserve Card, you get a first checked bag free. With the ever-increasing cost of a checked bag with Delta, this can really add up:

Depending on how many bags you’re checking, a few trips with a companion could pay for the card’s annual fee.

You can receive priority boarding just for having the Delta Reserve. This helps maximize your odds of finding space for your carry-on and getting to your seat sooner. To receive this benefit, you must ensure the primary cardmember’s SkyMiles number is linked to the reservation.

If you have the Delta Reserve Amex then you can save 20% in the form of a statement credit for eligible pre-purchased meals, and in-flight purchases of food, alcoholic beverages, and audio headsets, on Delta flights. Allow 8-12 weeks for the statement credit to post.

Delta has a Pay With Miles feature, where if you have a Delta co-branded credit card you can redeem miles for one cent each toward a Delta flight purchase (in increments of 5,000 miles per $50). That’s not the best deal in the world, though this is a feature that’s exclusively available to those with an eligible card.

Some people find this to be useful since they can redeem their miles toward flights, and then they still earn MQDs for taking those flights.

With the TakeOff 15 perk (exclusively for those with select Delta Amex cards), you can save 15% on the cost of a SkyMiles award ticket when traveling exclusively on Delta. Delta SkyMiles award pricing is dynamic, and generally you’ll find that each mile gets you a bit over a cent toward the cost of a ticket.

Saving 15% on these awards is valuable, and means that you’ll generally get somewhere around 1.2-1.3 cents of value per mile (or sometimes even more). In many cases this will end up being a better value than using the Pay With Miles option, so it’s a real perk of the card.

Having the Delta Reserve Card gets you priority for complimentary upgrades, assuming you have Medallion status. That’s because the card acts as a tiebreaker.

If you have the Reserve Card you get upgrade priority over other Medallion members within the same Medallion level and fare class. Given how competitive upgrades are, this can make a material difference in terms of whether you clear or not.

The Delta Reserve Card offers complimentary Delta First and Delta Comfort upgrades on eligible flights for non-elite members. You will be toward the bottom of the upgrade list, but there are lots of situations where this could help you score a good extra legroom seat, or in some cases even a first class seat.

Those with the Delta Reserve Card receive a Global Entry or TSA PreCheck credit. This benefit applies once every four years. This can save you big time both at security and immigration, and is something I highly recommend signing up for if eligible.

Just for having the Delta Reserve Card, you receive Hertz President’s Circle elite status, which is Hertz’s top-tier status. Status is valid for as long as you’re a cardmember. This should take the pain out of renting cars, and offers the following perks:

The Delta Reserve Card comes with a handful of coverage benefits that can protect you and your belongings both at home and on the road, including:

The maximum benefit amount for Trip Cancellation and Interruption Insurance is $10,000 per Covered Trip and $20,000 per Eligible Card per 12 consecutive month period. Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company. Up to $500 per Covered Trip that is delayed for more than 6 hours; and 2 claims per Eligible Card per 12 consecutive month period. Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company. Baggage insurance plan: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc. Extended warranty and purchase protection: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company.

One of the great features of Amex cards is access to Amex Offers, which offers savings or bonus points on purchases with all kinds of retailers. There’s huge value to be had in holding multiple Amex cards so that you can get these offers on multiple cards and enjoy a variety of offers across cards.

Amex Offers could save you hundreds of dollars per year. You can access these offers by logging into your account and scrolling down to the bottom of your account summary page.

The Delta Reserve Credit Card has a steep annual fee, but the card also offers great benefits. The card offers perks ranging from lounge access, to a companion certificate, to up to two free checked bags, to upgrade priority, to all kinds of credits, to the ability to spend your way to elite status.

This card isn’t for the casual Delta flyer, but for someone who flies Delta moderately or often, I’d say this card is well worth considering.

If the Delta Reserve Amex sounds interesting to you but you are instead looking for a card for your small business, consider the Delta SkyMiles® Reserve Business American Express Card.

Most of the benefits of the card are the same. One significant difference is that the business card earns 1.5x miles on all purchases after spending $150,000 annually, which could be useful for big spenders. Furthermore, the business card offers a $250 annual Delta Stays credit, rather than a $200 annual credit.

Many people might be trying to decide between the American Express Platinum Card® (learn more) and the Delta Reserve Card. The cards have some overlapping benefits:

Leisure carrier Allegiant is growing again, this time teaming up with merger partner Sun Country to grow its network.

The Las Vegas-based budget airline announced 11 new routes on Tuesday, with the service split between Allegiant and Sun Country.

Additionally, five routes will switch from one airline to the other — a tangible sign of the integration that’s slowly getting underway since the acquisition closed earlier this year.

The big winner in Tuesday’s announcement: Gulf Shores, Alabama.

The Gulf Coast destination — which Allegiant began flying to in 2025 — landed four new routes with Allegiant as well as one new route with Sun Country.

It’s a remarkable ramp for the Gulf Shores International Airport at Jack Edwards Field (GUF), which now has nonstop flights to 17 destinations, according to the airport’s website. The airport had no regular airline service at all prior to Allegiant’s arrival.

When Sun Country’s new service to Minneapolis-Saint Paul International Airport (MSP) begins April 16, it will mark the first time an airline other than Allegiant has scheduled service from the airport.

Elsewhere, Allegiant added two new Florida routes from the mid-Atlantic: one each from Philadelphia and Washington, D.C.

Sun Country will add nonstop service from O’Hare International Airport (ORD) to Asheville, North Carolina, and Knoxville, Tennessee — two destinations near the Great Smoky Mountains National Park that are already served by Allegiant.

Beyond the new routes, Allegiant is poised to take over service on four routes currently operated by Sun Country. Meanwhile, Sun Country will assume Allegiant’s Cincinnati-Denver route on May 27.

The changes will effectively add three new destinations to Sun Country's network: Belleville, Illinois, near St. Louis; Gulf Shores, Alabama; and Knoxville, Tennessee. Meanwhile, MSP — Sun Country's home base and main hub — will join Allegiant's route map.

"Minnesota is an essential part of the future of our combined company, and today's announcement is another step in delivering on that commitment," Allegiant CEO Greg Anderson said in a statement. "MSP is our largest base of operations by a wide margin, and we see opportunities for continued growth there."

Allegiant and Sun Country will continue to operate as separate brands at least into 2028 “or later,” Allegiant said in the press release. It will eventually move to a single brand.

For now, however, Allegiant touted Tuesday’s new service announcement as a preview of the expanded network that customers of the combined carrier will eventually be able to access.

"As we planned for summer 2027, our focus was on creating more opportunities for travelers by leveraging the complementary strengths of each airline's network while continuing to operate separately," Drew Wells, Allegiant's chief commercial officer, said in the company's statement.

“Just as importantly, these routes are a first look at how we'll create more options, access and value for our customers in the long term,” he added.

Full details on the new routes are below.

#6103. Threats to broadcasters hang over FCC nominee hearing

President Donald Trump's Republican nominee to the Federal Communications Commission faced opposition Tuesday from Senate Democrats who fear the commission could be controlled exclusively by Republicans under Chairman Brendan Carr, who they vowed to investigate in the next Congress.

Appearing before the Senate Commerce Committee, nominee Danielle Thumann Severs limited her commitments to independence from Carr, including on regulating broadcasters based on their content decisions.

Much of the hearing focused on Carr and his threats to use the FCC to punish broadcasters he disagrees with.

Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., said that he expects Carr will not last long in his position once Democrats take control of Congress in the new year.

“Mr. Carr, if you're listening now, know you're going to be in this body once a month, if not more, and in the House of Representatives as well, answering questions … so we can get to the bottom of the nonsense and the cover-ups that have been taking place,” Luján said.

The nomination of Thumann Severs, who currently serves as senior counsel to Carr, has led to consternation among Democrats due to continued vacancies at the FCC. The five-member commission is intended to have three members of the president’s party, including the chair, and two in the minority.

Currently Carr serves alongside fellow Republican Olivia Trusty and Democrat Anna M. Gomez, whose term expired earlier this year. Gomez may continue to serve through next year under the law if a replacement is not nominated and confirmed.

Democrats are concerned that if Thumann Severs were to be confirmed, the commission’s three Republican members could constitute a quorum on their own, allowing Trump to fire Gomez.

Sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., said Senate precedent is to move pairs of one Democratic and one Republican nominee for the FCC and that he “strongly” believed the Thumann Severs nomination should have been paired with a renomination of Gomez in order to continue having “both parties at the table.”

“A bipartisan FCC is essential to avoid things like large-scale media consolidation [and] I think also, more fundamentally, to protect a free and diverse press [that] serves everyone,” Hickenlooper said.

In addition to urging Trump to renominate Gomez, Democrats underlined the need for a second Democratic member of the commission.

Hickenlooper highlighted Thumann Severs’ close work with Carr, who Democrats and some Republicans have been critical of for comments about using the FCC’s public interest standard against television stations airing programming Carr disagrees with.

Thumann Severs’ work at the FCC currently focuses on the Wireline, Public Safety and Homeland Security, and Consumer and Governmental Affairs bureaus, rather than the Media Bureau.

Committee Chair Ted Cruz, R-Texas, has also been critical of Carr’s comments. On Tuesday, he listed the FCC’s request for ABC-owned stations to submit early license renewals alongside earlier incidents in which he said Democrats encouraged the weaponization of the FCC against conservative voices.

“The First Amendment places important limits on the government’s ability to regulate speech,” Cruz said. “The FCC possesses significant regulatory authority over communications, so there is always a risk that it could weaponize its authority against Americans with whom it disagrees.”

Thumann Severs committed to Cruz that she would base licensing decisions on “the law and the record” and not use the FCC’s authority to “pressure or punish” broadcasters for protected speech.

However, when Sen. Edward J. Markey, D-Mass., questioned Thumann Severs on whether the FCC could punish broadcasters the president disagreed with, Thumann Severs repeated one of Carr’s arguments in discussing the FCC’s role.

“Broadcasters are subject to public interest obligations as part of the public trustee model in exchange for the licenses that they hold,” she said. “As part of those public interest obligations, they are subject to many different rules and requirements, and the FCC is charged with enforcing and investigating the public interest standard against broadcasters.”

Under repeated questions from Markey about Carr’s previous remarks, Thumann Severs said she would base her decisions “in the facts and the law and the record.”

Luján also asked Thumann Severs to name issues where she had disagreed with Carr or Trump. While she said her decisions would be her own, she declined to name any examples of disagreement.

In addition to questions about Carr, Democrats asked the nominee about the FCC’s E-Rate program, which provides low-cost connectivity for schools and libraries, and the Universal Service Fund, which funds the E-Rate program and other programs.

Thumann Severs said that she believes the E-Rate program has been successful and that the FCC has a statutory obligation to provide some kind of discounted service to schools and libraries. But she was less forthcoming on whether the FCC could shut down the program as it currently exists without congressional approval or whether the program should be restricted only to rural areas.

Late last month, Democratic members of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, led by Communications and Technology Subcommittee ranking member Doris Matsui, D-Calif., sent a letter to Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and Cruz urging Gomez’s renomination with any move to confirm a Republican nominee.

“Commissioner Gomez has shown the experience and judgment to continue that work,” the members wrote. “We therefore ask that the Senate pair any new Republican nominee with her renomination to a full term, consistent with the bipartisan design Congress built into this agency.”

On Monday, the Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights also sent a letter to committee leadership urging a delay on the hearing and any vote on Thumann Severs’ nomination until Gomez can be renominated.

“Independent agencies should not be extensions of presidential will: their leaders should exercise independent judgement based on their expertise and statutory mandates,” the group wrote.

Cruz did not indicate Tuesday when the committee might vote on Thumann Severs’ nomination, and no markup has yet been announced by the committee of hers' and those of three others for two posts at NASA and one at the Transportation Department who also testified.

#6101. Buy Hilton Honors Points With 120% Bonus By November 21: Worth It?

Through November 21, 2026, Hilton Honors is offering a buy points promotion, which is the program’s best-ever bonus on purchasing points! While Hilton Honors ordinarily offers up to a 100% bonus on purchased points, this time around the program is offering up to a 120% bonus, which is a cost of 0.45 cents per point. This could represent a great value for hotel redemptions, especially with an immediate use in mind, as members can purchase up to 528,000 points in one transaction.

As always, I only recommend buying points with a short term use in mind, and if you understand the mechanics of how award redemptions with a program work, including what redemption costs are like.

Link: Buy Hilton Honors points with this promotion with a 120% bonus

Between 12AM ET on October 7 and 11:59PM ET on November 21, 2026, Hilton Honors is offering a bonus on purchased points. Different Hilton Honors members may be targeted for different bonuses, so you’ll want to log into your account to see what you’re eligible for. It would appear that the best offer is for up to a 120% bonus, and that’s structured as follows:

Hilton Honors ordinarily charges one cent per purchased point, including all taxes and fees. That’s before any discounts or bonuses. If you’re eligible for the 120% bonus and maxed out the offer, you’d receive a total of 528,000 points at a cost of $2,400, which is a rate of 0.45 cents per Hilton Honors point.

Ordinarily, Hilton Honors lets members buy up to 160,000 points per account per calendar year, before any bonuses. However, during this promotion, that cap has been increased by 50%, to 240,000 points. With a 120% bonus, that means you could purchase up to 528,000 points.

The purchase of Hilton Honors points is non-refundable, and points purchased don’t count toward elite status. Purchased points will post within 48 hours of finalizing the purchase (though in my experience, much faster than that).

While Hilton Honors has a strict limit on how many points you can buy, note that there are ways to acquire more points than that limit without violating the rules.

Hilton lets members combine points across accounts at no cost, so in reality you could acquire substantially more points by simply buying them across accounts and then consolidating them. Hilton Honors lets members transfer up to 500,000 points, and receive up to two million points, per calendar year. Each member can make up to six transfers to other members per calendar year, and new Hilton Honors members can only transfer or receive points a minimum of 30 days after enrollment.

Hilton also allows points pooling, whereby Hilton Honors members can combine points with up to 10 other members, with the same limitations.

When Hilton Honors offer a promotion on purchased points, it’s most common to see a 100% bonus (the equivalent of a 50% discount). So this 120% bonus is the best-ever promotion we’ve seen from the program, so that’s awesome.

Below is a chart with some of the recent buy points promotions we saw from the Hilton Honors program, before this one.

Hilton Honors point purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as a hotel purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. That means if you pay with a Hilton credit card, you wouldn’t earn any bonus rewards, so it’s not treated as if it’s Hilton spending.

I’d recommend using a card with which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. When in doubt, review which credit cards are best for buying points and miles.

There’s potentially huge value to be had buying Hilton Honors points. Hilton Honors sells points at a reasonable cost, has lots of aspirational properties, has good redemptions with a fifth night free opportunity, and elite status is also easy to earn with the program. Hilton’s partnership with Small Luxury Hotels of the World (SLH) is also awesome, and offers great redemption opportunities.

However, people shouldn’t blindly buy Hilton Honors points, as there are also lots of redemptions where you won’t come out ahead. As I see it, the biggest value with buying Hilton Honors is for aspirational redemptions at expensive properties. Let me give some examples, based on current redemption rates.

For example, take the Waldorf Astoria Maldives, which is bookable for 250,000 points per night for a standard room. At a rate of 0.45 cents per point, you could acquire those points for $1,125. As a point of comparison, the cash rate would be $3,400, so that’s like two-thirds off. That’s pretty amazing!

As another example, take the Waldorf Astoria Los Cabos, which is bookable for 250,000 points per night for a standard room. At a rate of 0.45 cents per point, you could acquire those points for $1,125. As a point of comparison, the cash rate would be close to $2,200, so that’s like half off.

Above I mentioned the Hilton Honors partnership with SLH, so let me give an example there. RiverView Ranch Retreat is located in Montana, and is bookable for 220,000 points per night for a standard room. At a rate of 0.45 cents per point, you could acquire those points for $990. As a point of comparison, the cash rate would be over $3,800 (the screenshot below is for two nights, since that’s the minimum stay), so that’s close to three-fourths off.

Now, while the above are all examples of what a good deal it can be to buy Hilton Honors points, let me of course acknowledge that these are all top-end properties. Unfortunately I find that for your run of the mill Hilton properties, including many limited service hotels, the value just isn’t there in the same way.

For example, take the Hilton Garden Inn Tampa, which is bookable for 45,000 points per night. At a rate of 0.45 cents per point, you could acquire those points for $203. As a point of comparison, the cash rate would be under $180, so there’s absolutely no reason to buy points, only to redeem them for less value than what you paid. You’ll find that to be pretty common, which is why I always recommend crunching the numbers before making a purchase.

Hilton Honors doesn’t have a published award chart, but rather the program has dynamic award pricing. This means that the cost of a standard free night award can vary depending on the day of the week, time of year, etc.

As a general rule of thumb, Hilton Honors free night awards start at 10,000 points per night, and go up to 250,000 points per night (which is a shame, because up until last year, properties maxed out at 150,000 points per night).

Sometimes you’ll see award costs that are way higher than these amounts. In those situations it’s because there’s not a standard room available, so higher pricing kicks in for premium rooms. That’s generally not nearly as good of a use of Hilton Honors points, and you’ll find that some awards even cost one million or more points per night. Obviously that’s a lousy value.

If you have Hilton Honors elite status (which is easy to earn, as I’ll outline below), you receive a fifth night free on award redemptions. This is a way to stretch your points even further, and whenever possible, I’d recommend making your Hilton Honors award stays in increments of five nights.

To take advantage of this, just log into your Hilton Honors elite account, and go through the process of making an award booking for five nights. When you get to the booking page, you should notice that the cost of the fifth night is automatically deducted.

Let me give an example how much value this can add. Say you want to book five nights at the Waldorf Astoria Seychelles Platte Island. At a rate of 150,000 points per night, you’d pay a total of 600,000 points for five nights, which averages out to 120,000 points per night. At a rate of 0.45 cents per point, that’s like the equivalent of paying $540 per night. As a point of comparison, the cash rate would be over $1,800 per night, so that represents absolutely massive savings.

One thing I love about the program is how easy it is to earn elite status with credit cards, including both Hilton Honors™ Gold Status and Hilton Honors™ Diamond Status. These tiers offer perks like room upgrades, complimentary breakfast, hotel credits, and more. For example:

Hilton Honors points don’t expire as long as you have at least some account activity once every 24 months. Eligible account activity includes earning or redeeming points, so buying points would even reset the expiration of your points.

Everyone will value points differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Hilton Honors points to be worth 0.5 cents each, and I tend to value points pretty conservatively. As you can see, the pricing here is potentially better than what I value these points, and there are lots of ways to get outsized value with this promotion.

Hilton Honors doesn’t have blackout dates on award nights, and all standard rooms are available for award redemptions. So this is about as good of a policy as you’ll find with any hotel group when it comes to award room availability.

There are lots of ways to earn Hilton Honors points, beyond just staying at Hilton properties or buying the points directly. You can easily earn points by using Hilton Honors’ co-branded credit cards, which also offer great welcome bonuses. These cards include the following:

You can also transfer points from Amex Membership Rewards to Hilton Honors (at a 1:2 ratio), and from Bilt Rewards to Hilton Honors (at a 1:1 ratio). I wouldn’t consider either of those redemptions to represent a good deal. That’s simply because I value Hilton Honors points at 0.5 cents each, while I value those points currencies at 1.7 cents each, so the math just doesn’t work out.

Hilton Honors is currently offering a best-ever bonus on purchased points, whereby members can receive up to a 120% bonus, which is an opportunity to acquire points for 0.45 cents each. In the past we’ve generally seen bonuses of up to 100%, so this is a better offer than ever before. In fairness, Hilton Honors points have also been devalued a bit over time. With a short term use in mind, there are plenty of situations where this could represent a good deal.

Do you plan on buying Hilton Honors points with a bonus?

#6100. Ranked: Which Of United Airlines' US Hubs Run The Best Operation In 2026?

United Airlines operates the largest fleet of jetliners in the world, serving one of the world’s most expansive and complex networks of air routes. To keep domestic commuters and international flyers moving, UA contends with harsh weather, air traffic control failures, and other unexpected disruptions across roughly 4,500 daily departures at its top hubs. This countdown examines the hard data to reveal how airfields from the West Coast to the Windy City, Big Apple, Lone Star State, and even the nation's capital stack up.

According to Delay Atlas, Chicago O'Hare is at the very bottom for on-time performance (OTP). It is the network's worst-performing hub, with only 73% of United flights arriving as expected in 2025. Tight flight schedules and congested skies quickly collapse during summer thunderstorms in the Midwest. Meanwhile, winter snow and ice pose another seasonal weather obstacle. The airport as a whole ranks approximately 24th this year among major US airports.

Traveling in the morning normally goes smoothly, but as the day goes on, delays mount quickly. Last year, nearly 90% of flights departing between 5:00 AM and 8:00 AM did so on time. By the busy evening rush between 5:00 PM and 8:00 PM, on-time departures (OTD) dropped below 70%. Traffic jams on the tarmac often force arriving planes to sit on the ramp waiting for an open gate.

All that waiting on the ground creates big headaches for both the airline and passengers. A Boeing 737 sitting with its engines idling burns roughly 1,000 to 1,200 pounds (454 to 544 kg) of fuel every hour just waiting to move. Those delays can even cause pilots to time out of legal working hours and force a crew swap. In the worst-case scenario, travelers could be left stranded without their checked bags, making ORD the biggest drag on United's schedule.

Last year, United canceled 2.3% of its Newark schedule, the highest cancellation percentage of any United hub, and just 76.3% of its flights landed on time. Despite the sound of slot restrictions, the airport's overall rise to fifth place in the country for punctuality was aided by federal regulations. The cap set a ceiling of 72 takeoffs and landings each hour, and yet UA still has trouble here, despite OTD rising to 79.0% in 2026.

Situated in one of the busiest air corridors in the nation, the airport only has a small footprint to operate out of. The confined airfield leaves almost no room for error. When bad weather hits the East Coast, air traffic slows to a crawl. That's when UA often has to cancel flights outright rather than let planes circle in the air. Major runway construction made things even tighter, temporarily cutting flights down to 28 per hour and forcing UA to trim its peak schedules to prevent gridlock on the apron.

To carry as many travelers as possible without breaking the strict FAA hourly flight cap, UA employs its biggest jets for domestic trips as well as overseas itineraries. The airline flies Boeing 777 widebodies, which weigh over 304,500 pounds (138,119 kg), between Newark and San Francisco. Using one giant twin-aisle instead of two smaller narrowbodies lets United move hundreds more people at once while saving precious takeoff spots and gate space.

A closer look at the revamped Simple Flying Flight Tracker and its sleek, user-friendly redesign that makes navigating live flight data a breeze.

With almost 108,000 flights passing through its ramp in 2025, Denver claims the title as United's busiest hub. The airline reported a network-best cancellation rate of only 0.41% and a strong 78.9% on-time arrival (OTA) rate despite the heavy demand. Air traffic control can also land and launch a higher volume of jets than at airports like Newark without creating ground gridlock, thanks to Denver's generous real estate.

The airport is situated on expansive plains with six runways that never overlap, maximizing ground operations efficiency. Although the airport layout is ideal for dense schedules, Denver's high altitude presents a weather hurdle in summer. Sitting 5,434 feet (1,656 meters) above sea level, the air is already thinner than at coastal airports. On hot summer afternoons, that thin, warm air behaves as if it were over 9,000 feet (2,743 meters) high in a turbofan engine.

The low density and high temperature make it much harder for jet engines to pull in enough air to produce takeoff thrust. On a heavy Boeing 737 MAX, the engines have to spin at over 100% N1 and can push internal exhaust temperatures close to 1,832°F (1,000°C) just to get off the ground. That burns more gas on every sortie and compounds wear and tear on the planes.

United Airlines has postponed the launch of these routes due to FAA restrictions.

San Francisco delivered a low cancellation rate of 0.46% and a strong 79.8% OTA rate in 2025. However, with an average OTD of only 73.42%, SFO came in 19th place in the country overall. The airport's design is to blame for recent drops in hourly flight volumes. The FAA revoked the parallel landing exemption that allowed simultaneous operations of its two main arrival runways, which lie only 750 feet (229 meters) apart.

The two strips are 3,550 feet (1,082 meters) below the standard FAA separation limit. That forced the agency to prohibit two aircraft from landing side by side in low clouds. The long-standing exemption ended this March following a broader federal safety review sparked by the January 2025 midair collision of American Airlines Flight 5342. Thus, when the famous Bay Area fog rolls in, arrival capacity immediately drops from 60 planes per hour down to about 30.

That sudden slowdown forces air traffic controllers to hold flights back at their departure cities across the country, creating ripple-effect delays throughout the day. Once planes finally clear the fog, the cool conditions actually help United's biggest jets take off. Long international flights across the Pacific rely heavily on the Boeing 777-300ER, which can weigh up to 775,000 pounds (351,534 kg) at takeoff when fueled for a transpacific voyage.

In light of the recent disruptions caused by the FAA's nationwide ground stop in the US, I wanted to take a minute and discuss what are the longest delays that you have ever experienced? What were the results of the delays, and did you get rebooked on another airline or not? In terms of delays, the longest I've experienced was with American Airlines, when a flight I was set to take from Heathrow to Chicago was delayed by over six hours. Because I would have missed my connection to JFK (last flight of the day from ORD to JFK at that), I rebooked myself onto a flight to Charlotte. My flight from CLT to JFK ended up being delayed, then canceled, and I was rebooked on a flight to Newark the following morning. After my overnight stay at the airport, the Newark flight was canceled, and I was placed on standby for a flight to LaGuardia, which cleared. Do you have any delay or cancellation stories to share? What was your longest delay, and has it impacted your perception of the airline?

United's primary hub for the Southern US and Latin America is Houston Intercontinental. The field handled over 74,200 flights last year, with an 80.6% on-time rate and a low cancellation rate of 0.55%. In terms of punctuality, the airport as a whole rose to sixth position in the country, highlighting how a large hub can still run efficiently when the layout is optimized for high traffic on the ramp.

ATC can coordinate large waves of aircraft without causing taxiway congestion thanks to the five runways and extensive taxiway grid. When summer storms shut down Chicago or crowded skies slow down Newark, UA can use Houston as a backup to relieve pressure. Rerouting connecting travelers through Texas helps keep the rest of the network moving. Wide taxiways keep planes rolling steadily to their gates, preventing backups during the busy afternoon rush.

Houston is also a primary home base for UA's newest single-aisle aircraft, the Airbus A321neo. Built with lightweight metal alloys and powered by next-generation engines, these planes cut costs and emissions with lower fuel burn on busy daily routes while giving travelers a quieter, more modern cabin experience.

Our Flight Tracker is now embeddable, letting any site display live flight data instead of a screenshot. Here's how to add it in three easy steps.

Dulles avoids many weather-related ground delays, in contrast to other East Coast hubs that come to a complete stop during summer storms. With an 82.1% on-time arrival percentage and a low 0.85% cancellation rate across approximately 37,000 flights, Washington Dulles established itself as United's top-performing fortress hub in 2025. In terms of departure timeliness, the airport as a whole rose to second place in the country and is looking to improve, with 82.2% OTD in 2026 so far.

The airport has a significant edge over congested competitors like Newark due to its runway and taxiway configuration. Four wide strips that don't intersect make it possible for controllers to run high-volume operations, even when clouds and rain roll through the area. Arriving flights from Europe can land without circling the field, while domestic flights push back from the gates and take off without obstructing arriving jets.

United is increasingly using its Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner to maximize comfort on busy cross-country flights from Dulles to the West Coast. The plane's lightweight carbon-fiber materials allow the cabin to be pressurized closer to ground level, enabling a cabin altitude of 6,000 feet (1,829 meters), rather than 8,000 feet (2,438 meters) on older planes. Combining that atmosphere with higher humidity, smart lights, and quieter walls greatly reduces jet lag.

The routes appear to have been removed temporarily.

Los Angeles International is the most consistent and dependable operating base for United. The airline completed around 30,000 flights in the last year with an 82.5% OTA rate and a 0.50% cancellation rate, but LAX has slipped to 79% OTA in 2026, per JohnnyJet. UA's Los Angeles business focuses mostly on direct, point-to-point flights, as opposed to mega-hubs like Chicago or Denver, which rely on massive waves of connecting passengers.

LAX functions primarily as a massive Origin-and-Destination market, meaning most passengers begin or end their trips in Los Angeles rather than connecting through. Because UA runs a smaller, leaner schedule here than at mega-hubs like Denver or Chicago, operations rely less on tightly packed connecting waves where a single late inbound plane triggers a domino effect of missed connections.

Additionally, United's $573 million renovation of Terminal 7 streamlined gate layouts, boarding areas, and baggage handling, giving the airline modern infrastructure to turn aircraft around quickly.

#6098. Rift grows among Senate Democrats over who will lead in majority

More Democrats emerged Tuesday wanting someone besides Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., to lead their conference in the majority.

But Schumer maintained confidence he would be reelected to the post despite Sens. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., publicly calling for a different leader or a “concrete plan” that provides change.

“I’m confident I will be elected majority leader, and our caucus is really united in focusing on bringing down costs, on ending the corruption, on ending the chaos, on ending the war,” Schumer told reporters Tuesday. “We have great unity in our caucus, and I’ll be proud to lead it.”

Sanders said during a news conference Tuesday the election was about “change and the need for the Democratic Party to move in a new and bold direction.”

“I personally have known Chuck Schumer for over 30 years, and I like Chuck. Nobody works harder than Chuck Schumer. But in my view the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck to be reelected as the Democratic leader,” Sanders said, calling for an “economy that works for all, not just the people on top.”

“Do I think Chuck has been leading in that direction?” he asked. “No.”

Some incoming members and now incumbents have pointed to Maryland Democrat Chris Van Hollen as one possibility to challenge Schumer. Van Hollen had previously thrown cold water on the idea by saying he was instead “kicking the tires” on a presidential run in 2028 but has recently changed his tune.

A person familiar with Van Hollen’s thinking said he “has received an outpouring of calls on running for majority leader and is now in active listening mode.”

Slotkin did not endorse anyone for leader but said she had a “really productive conversation” with Van Hollen yesterday.

“Whoever wants my vote is going to have to show me a concrete plan that’s definitely different. I’m a ‘no’ until and unless I see that from anyone,” she said, urging her peers to “withhold quorum” when Senate Democrats hold their leadership elections “until you get that plan and you feel like you have a voice in that plan.”

She urged not just a roadmap for the first 100 days, but ideas for how to “communicate differently.” As for her own future, she said, “I am not actively seeking this job. I’m seeking change.”

Asked about his plans Monday evening, Van Hollen said, “It’s not about me, but I am listening to the thousands of people who have been calling for change, but especially listening to our members, with a particular ear to new members who have just come off the campaign trail.”

“What I’ve said from the very beginning is, we shouldn’t have a coronation. We should have a caucus discussion about what we're going to do with the power and responsibilities that have been invested in us,” Van Hollen said. “I’m in listening mode and haven’t shut the door.”

Van Hollen took it a step further at an event Tuesday in Washington, D.C., criticizing the minority leader and Democrats’ campaign arm over their preferences in some primaries. “Schumer and the DSCC sided with the crypto industry and AIPAC against these candidates,” he said, according to a livestream of the event.

Schumer tried to tamp down the suggestion of a rivalry. “We talk frequently, and we’re united — united in lowering costs, and united in ending this damn war,” he said of Van Hollen.

Others threw their support behind Schumer ahead of the Democratic leadership elections, which are expected to take place in December.

Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., praised Schumer for raising money and recruiting candidates like Sens.-elect Sherrod Brown of Ohio and Roy Cooper of North Carolina to help land at minimum seven seats, and potentially nine if Alaska and Mississippi ultimately swing their way.

“That takes vision. It takes clarity of thought. It takes strategic leadership, and that is what Sen. Schumer has done. And that is why you will see, despite all grumblings, enormous gratitude,” she said.

Gillibrand pointed to candidates like Scott Colom, the Democrat in Mississippi who is currently leading GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in a nail-biter of a race. “That wave doesn’t get created by magic. It gets created by hard work and putting the pieces together over years,” she said.

Colom, however, has been noncommittal, telling MS NOW, “Too many of our leaders are from the same areas of the country,” pointing to the Brooklyn roots of both Schumer and current House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to run for speaker on the House side.

Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., said he and Schumer have had their differences. But he implied he backs him for majority leader: “At the end of the day, these are historic numbers. It’s time for us to unify. We are going to work together as a caucus to plan together about how to move forward for what the country wants us to do, and I think we have the person who I think is going to lead us there.”

Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., said Democrats have “an opportunity to do things differently, and I think we will, regardless of who the leader is. It doesn’t really matter whose name is on the door.”

“Yes,” he said of his support for Schumer, noting that so far, nobody has officially stepped up to the plate. “This is a guy that worked incredibly hard over the last couple of years. I know people have other opinions about this. But we have a mandate to do things and get things done for the American people.”

Mark Schoeff Jr., Paul M. Krawzak and Kelly Livingston contributed to this report.

The Chase Ultimate Rewards program is currently offering a bonus for points transfers to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. While I’d only transfer points with a specific use in mind, there’s huge value to be had here, as a 40% transfer bonus is massive.

Between November 16 and December 30, 2026, it’s possible to receive a 40% bonus when transferring Chase Ultimate Rewards points to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club.

This promotion is being offered on Chase’s end (in the United States), and is hard coded into the transfer ratio, meaning you should see the bonus at the time that you make the transfer. You can take advantage of this offer an unlimited number of times. Transfers from Chase to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club are generally instant.

We see a bonus like this to Virgin Atlantic a few times per year. We last saw a transfer bonus over the summer, so it hasn’t been a long gap at all. Past transfer bonuses have been in the range of 25-40%, so this is at the very top end of that spectrum.

There are several great cards earning Chase Ultimate Rewards points, and it’s easy to combine points between the cards.

Virgin Atlantic is a frequent flyer program with more niche redemption opportunities. In addition to being able to redeem Flying Club points for travel on Virgin Atlantic (with steep carrier imposed surcharges), there’s also good value to be had for redemptions on Air New Zealand, All Nippon Airways, and Delta, as well as more broadly on SkyTeam airlines.

Nowadays Flying Club has dynamic award pricing for travel on Virgin Atlantic. What’s exciting is that on the low end, redemption rates are very attractive, and it’s possible to fly Virgin Atlantic Upper Class between the United States and United Kingdom for under 30,000 points, in some situations. And that’s before a transfer bonus.

Beyond that, Virgin Atlantic has several airline partners, some of which are more lucrative than others. Probably the best use of Flying Club points is for travel in ANA first & business class. You can find the redemption rates below.

Paying 45,000-47,500 Flying Club points for a one-way business class ticket between the United States and Japan is a phenomenal value to start with. Then when you consider the 40% transfer bonus, that means you could be paying significantly fewer Chase points. First class can also be a good deal.

All Nippon Airways’ new first & business class are amazing products as well. The major catch is that availability can be really tough to come by.

Through December 30, 2026, you can receive a 40% bonus when you transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards points to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. This is more of a niche program, but with a specific use in mind, there’s a lot of value to be had.

With the 40% bonus, you can potentially get some incredible redemption values for travel on Virgin Atlantic, including in Upper Class. There’s also significant value to be had if redeeming on partners, whether it’s on a SkyTeam partner, or on one of Virgin Atlantic’s non-SkyTeam partner airlines.
