#6063. Delta CEO’s Cope: Ed Bastian Says Doesn’t Need Starlink, Current Wi-Fi Good Enough

Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian says “customers are not choosing airlines based on the Wi-Fi.” That’s a remarkable claim from an airline that’s spent years promoting free internet as a reason to choose its premium experience. Speaking at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit on Monday, Bastian defended passing on Starlink and waiting for Amazon Leo which is still unproven and whose timetable is now in question. He downplayed competitors’ progress, argued Delta’s current Viasat service comes close enough, and expressed confidence that Amazon would match or beat Starlink. It was pure cope. Delta doesn’t plan to begin installing Amazon until 2028 and that’s if the service works and delivers on schedule. United and Southwest both plan to finish their Starlink installations in 2027, and American is adding the service as well (so are Alaska and even Frontier). Delta’s Wifi Was Fine When Fewer People Used It Delta’s Viasat internet was fine when a few people on each flight were paying to use it. Make it free, get a much larger share of the plane online, and the experience can become unusable. I wrote about this last December after flying Delta to Las Vegas. The system repeatedly bogged down until nothing would load. I’d rather pay for internet that works than get free internet that doesn’t. Bandwidth has to be shared. Removing the price doesn’t create more capacity, but it gives a lot more people a reason to connect. A connection that works well with light use just isn’t the same thing – and Starlink’s low earth orbit satellites simply give the signal less distance to travel, delivering almost no latency. Bastian points to two new Viasat satellites. ViaSat-3 F3 entered service in August, and F2 entered service in September. But Delta’s own current wifi explanation acknowledges that performance varies with customer demand and satellite capacity, with less consistent service in high-demand or capacity-constrained areas. The airline knows this problem exists, which is why they’re touting Amazon’s service as a future improvement. United And Southwest Are Already Flying Starlink Bastian suggests most airlines promoting Starlink haven’t started yet. He doesn’t identify which airlines he’s counting. Here’s what the competitors actually say: United Airlines: More than half its daily flights already have Starlink. It expects nearly 64% by year-end and completion of installations by the end of 2027. Southwest Airlines: Its latest quarterly filing confirms equipped aircraft are already in service, with the full fleet expected to be finished in fall 2027. Last week it publicized gaming and livestreaming aboard a flight from Austin to San Diego. Alaska and Hawaiian: The group’s October 26 installation update shows all 93 Embraer 175s, Hawaiian’s 18 Airbus A321neos and 24 Airbus A330s equipped, along with 16 Boeing 737 MAX aircraft. Even Southwest expects to have Starlink throughout its fleet before Delta starts putting Amazon on its first 500 aircraft. That’s an awkward comparison for the airline charging a premium when it’ll be universal on the only U.S. airline without first class even. Wifi Doesn’t Have To Decide Every Ticket To Cost Delta Money I explained last month that I’ve avoided United and Southwest when I couldn’t count on functional internet. Starlink changes that calculation. I’ll pay more to work onboard because losing several productive hours costs more than the airfare savings. Recon Analytics finds wifi ranks among the top five business-trip airline selection factors for 32.6% of flyers, and first for 6.5%. Even among leisure travelers, 3.8% rank it first. Delta doesn’t need to lose everyone. It can lose a few expensive trips from customers who fly often, buy premium seats and carry airline credit cards. That’s precisely the business it wants. United is already using wifi to recruit those customers. It says its wifi-focused status match campaign produced a tenfold increase in daily applications. Amazon Still Has To Deliver. Bastian says that when Delta gets Amazon Leo, “we’ll be at least as good as Starlink if not better.” He hasn’t demonstrated that. Amazon needs enough satellites in the right orbits, working aircraft equipment, certification, and an airline installation program. It then has to deliver consistently with actual passengers using it. Delta’s own materials make the 2028 start subject to technical, certification and deployment milestones. And 2028 is the start of installations on an initial 500 aircraft. As I covered yesterday, Sunday’s failed Vulcan launch lost 40 Amazon satellites. We don’t yet know whether that pushes back Delta’s rollout. But the risk extends beyond replacing those satellites: Amazon contracted for 38 Vulcan missions to launch more than 1,500 of them. Amazon’s prelaunch photo shows the satellites stacked for that mission. Bastian’s account of testing Starlink is consistent with reporting from 2022. Delta had an early look at the product. It chose different commercial terms. I’ve covered the dispute over Delta’s branded portal. And last month Bastian said the branding disagreement out loud: “(Elon) thought it should be called Starlink on the planes. I said ‘No, it’s gotta be Delta.’” Amazon could offer a broader deal involving cloud computing and entertainment. Delta also gets to keep directing passengers through its own platform, where it promotes partners and sells them things. But a cheaper contract has to save enough to cover the business lost while passengers wait. If someone moves expensive flights to United, earns status there and starts spending on a United credit card, Delta may have to buy that loyalty back long after Amazon finally arrives. Delta also gets to keep directing passengers through its own platform, where it promotes partners and sells them things. But a cheaper contract has to save enough to cover the business lost while passengers wait. If someone moves expensive flights to United, earns status there and starts spending on a United credit card, Delta may have to buy that loyalty back long after Amazon finally arrives. I explained last month that I’ve avoided United and Southwest when I couldn’t count on functional internet. Starlink changes that calculation. I’ll pay more to work onboard because losing several productive hours costs more than the airfare savings.

Recon Analytics finds wifi ranks among the top five business-trip airline selection factors for 32.6% of flyers, and first for 6.5%. Even among leisure travelers, 3.8% rank it first.

Delta doesn’t need to lose everyone. It can lose a few expensive trips from customers who fly often, buy premium seats and carry airline credit cards. That’s precisely the business it wants.

United is already using wifi to recruit those customers. It says its wifi-focused status match campaign produced a tenfold increase in daily applications.

Bastian says that when Delta gets Amazon Leo, “we’ll be at least as good as Starlink if not better.” He hasn’t demonstrated that. Amazon needs enough satellites in the right orbits, working aircraft equipment, certification, and an airline installation program. It then has to deliver consistently with actual passengers using it. Delta’s own materials make the 2028 start subject to technical, certification and deployment milestones. And 2028 is the start of installations on an initial 500 aircraft. As I covered yesterday, Sunday’s failed Vulcan launch lost 40 Amazon satellites. We don’t yet know whether that pushes back Delta’s rollout. But the risk extends beyond replacing those satellites: Amazon contracted for 38 Vulcan missions to launch more than 1,500 of them. Amazon’s prelaunch photo shows the satellites stacked for that mission. Bastian’s account of testing Starlink is consistent with reporting from 2022. Delta had an early look at the product. #6062. Deadline looms for post-9/11 FirstNet reauthorization

Supporters of the FirstNet program that provides emergency communications for first-responders still see hope for reauthorization this year, despite continued disagreements over what changes, if any, should be made to how the program is governed.

A House-passed reauthorization bill would shift authority toward the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and away from the FirstNet board, which is made up in part by first-responders.

The potential change is opposed by the influential Fraternal Order of Police, but any new bill or amendment would require floor votes in both the House and Senate, a potentially tall order as the 119th Congress draws to a close.

Authority for FirstNet, a program developed in the wake of 9/11, is set to expire in February of 2027 unless lawmakers pass an extension.

The program’s governing entity, the First Responder Network Authority, was created in 2012 in response to recommendations after the terrorist attacks, during which public safety agencies using different radio systems and overloaded phone lines struggled to adequately communicate.

The House passed its bipartisan reauthorization bill in April via voice vote. Senators have not yet taken up that legislation or introduced their own. In January, the Senate Commerce Committee’s Telecommunications and Media Subcommittee held a hearing on the program.

Related: First-responder network reauthorization advances

Craig Wheeler, a spokesman for subcommittee Chair Deb Fischer, R-Neb., said in a statement this week that reauthorization is still a priority.

“Sen. Fischer has been working closely with Chair Cruz on a bill and is having bipartisan discussions with Ranking Member Cantwell,” Wheeler said, referring to Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Maria Cantwell, D-Wash.

“Moving a bill as soon as possible remains a top priority for Sen. Fischer, including getting it through both chambers and signed into law by President Trump.”

The House bill would extend authority for FirstNet through fiscal 2037, stagger terms on the authority’s board and require five members of the board with public safety backgrounds, rather than three as needed under current law.

At issue in the reauthorization debate, in part, is control of the First Responder Network Authority.

The House bill would eliminate language in current law that established FirstNet as an “independent” authority within the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and would require the administration’s approval for most non-planning or emergency actions, though the bill was amended to include a list of actions the network can take without NTIA approval.

The changes are meant to respond to reports from the Commerce Department's Office of Inspector General that found that the AT&T-run service was not sufficiently available during the Maui wildfires in 2023 and that senior officials of the FirstNet Authority attempted to interfere with audits.

The Maui report noted the small number of FirstNet subscriptions among state and local first responders in the area and in an op-ed earlier this year, Maui Fire Chief Brad Ventura said his department was “not using FirstNet devices” at the time of the fires but is now adopting them. He also supported reauthorization in the op-ed.

Related: First-responders network faced with calls for change

But the shifting of control drew opposition from the Fraternal Order of Police, which prior to the bill’s committee markup urged its members to instead support a “clean reauthorization” of the program.

Jim Pasco, executive director of the FOP, emphasized his group’s desire to see decisions made by the FirstNet board, rather than by NTIA. He said that moving authority away from a group that is required to include first-responders would be “a threat to officer and public safety.”

Yucel Ors, legislative director for public safety and crime prevention at the National League of Cities, said that his group, along with the International Association of Fire Chiefs and other state and local government and public safety groups, worked closely with the House, including on the changes to put some “everyday controls and functions” back directly under the board’s control.

He said the National League of Cities supported the House bill, but that they hope that any changes made to FirstNet’s governance are “not going to impact the day-to-day operations that public safety depend on, rely on, and expect.”

Ors said he expects the Senate would make changes to the House-passed bill, but he doesn’t know if those changes would come in the form of an amendment or an entirely new bill.

No proposed Senate amendment to the House bill, or alternative Senate bill, has yet to emerge.

He expressed concern over the timeline for reauthorization, especially if the Senate doesn’t take up the House bill as is.

A new Senate bill or amendment would require votes in both the House and Senate, with floor time dwindling as both chambers work through must-pass legislation before the end of the year.

Congress could potentially pass a short-term reauthorization of FirstNet. Ors expressed worry that option could jeopardize the public-private relationship with contractor AT&T.

Pasco said he would prefer a short reauthorization over the House-passed bill, but said he hopes a full reauthorization could still pass this Congress.

The House bill has strong bipartisan support and the Senate’s negotiations are also bipartisan. Both Ors and Pasco expressed confidence that if time runs out this year for a reauthorization bill, a new version of the legislation would still have strong prospects under a Democratic Congress.

Additional context regarding the role of FirstNet during the Maui fires was added to this report.

#6061. Skift Commerce Summit 2026: Balancing Trust, Access, and Control in the Traveler Relationship

Travel companies are now being forced to decide which parts of the customer relationship to pursue directly while allowing and even enabling intermediaries to have more control of the journey.

AI is already searching and booking on behalf of travelers, but travel companies haven’t settled who should control those transactions, who should pay for them, or who takes primary responsibility for customer service.

At the Skift Commerce Summit, executives said AI is moving faster than the industry can settle the economics or rules around it.

“The agents are here,” said Skift Head of Research Seth Borko. “But almost no one is ready.”

Travel companies are now being forced to decide which parts of the customer relationship

Very Online is your best source for news about online travel, from startups to the biggest online travel agencies.

By submitting this form, you agree to receive email communication from Skift.

See more essential travel news in your search results.

Photo Caption: Skift's Rafat Ali opening the Skift Commerce Summit in New York City on November 11, 2026.

Skift provides the insights. You make the decisions.

Decision intelligence for travel leaders.

At the Skift Commerce Summit, executives said AI agents are already searching and booking travel, but the industry hasn't settled who controls those transactions, who pays for them, or who handles customer service when something goes wrong. United Airlines announced during the Summit that it would restrict AI agents from accessing its website, and MCR Hotels CEO Tyler Morse said MCR would ban them too if it could figure out how. Turkish Airlines took the opposite position: about 1% of its traffic already comes from AI, and digital chief Fatih Durmaz said the airline's stance is "very much to work with AI," while acknowledging that servicing and permissions still need substantial work. Skift Head of Research Seth Borko showed how an AI agent completed a United booking on a United credit card, then failed to earn miles because the transaction wasn't recognized correctly. Luxury Escapes CEO Adam Schwab said an AI customer-service system misunderstood a request and canceled a booking, costing about $10,000 to fix. The economics remain unresolved: Kalibri CEO Cindy Estis Green said U.S. hotels spent about $47 billion acquiring guests in 2025, roughly 25% of room revenue for most properties, and she was skeptical AI would lower that. JetBlue President Marty St. George said he fears intermediaries will eventually want to get paid, money airlines aren't spending today.

#6060. FAA’s Flight Shutdown Fuels A $30 Billion Funding Push—Most Of The Money Isn’t Even For Air Traffic Control

After the FAA communications breakdown brought departures across the country to a halt on Friday, the travel industry has its answer: give air traffic control another $30 billion. Most of the money in the bill they’re pushing wouldn’t even go to air traffic control. The U.S. Travel Association says Friday’s ground stop demonstrates that the FAA “lacks the resources necessary to modernize America’s aging aviation infrastructure.” It wants Congress to pass the Modern Skies Act sponsored by Senator Eric Schmitt (R-MO) before the end of this Congress. That legislation would provide $30.1 billion, including $15 billion for airport terminals. It would leave the FAA running air traffic control under essentially the same institutional structure that’s spent decades failing to deliver promised improvements. We need modern equipment. We also need to modernize the organization buying and operating it. Using this failure to sell airport terminal subsidies does neither particularly well. A Local Equipment Change Disrupted Most Of The National Network The nationwide departure stop began at 3:54 p.m. Eastern Friday and lasted until 8:15 p.m. The airline recovery took much longer. There were over 18,000 cancellations from Friday through Sunday. Planes and crews wound up in the wrong places. Crew duty limits and missed connections kept the disruption going after communications stabilized. The FAA identifies two sites: a radio facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, where contractor L3Harris was installing a router, and a radar facility in Amarillo, Texas. Excessive connection attempts flooded their ancient private network, disrupting aircraft communications and radar feeds at 17 of 22 en route centers and spreading into approach control facilities. Blocking the two sites stabilized the network. Officials also disabled the broadcasting function on about 60 similar routers. Some radio frequencies and radar feeds kept working, allowing aircraft already airborne to land. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford describes the work as routine maintenance, separate from the new $12.5 billion modernization program. That makes the question about managing the system day to day even more pressing if it can destabilize the whole system with only the third nationwide ground stop in U.S. history. Most Of The $30 Billion Would Go To Airports John Kefaliotis at Reason Foundation breaks down the spending. The introduced bill, S. 5572: Purpose Funding Terminal rebuilding pilot for up to three airports $10 billion Other airport terminal grants $5 billion Discretionary airport improvement grants $3 billion Common automation platform and controller workstation $7.2 billion Cloud computing and associated telecommunications $2 billion Air traffic control facilities, including digital towers $2 billion Air traffic flow management technology $600 million Consolidating terminal air traffic control facilities $300 million That’s $12.1 billion for air traffic control systems and facilities, versus $18 billion for airports. About 40% goes to air traffic control. The administration’s announcement includes building airports, but the sales pitch after Friday’s failure is that Congress needs to fund the air traffic control fix. The $10 billion terminal pilot is particularly brazen. It would cover up to 90% of costs at no more than three medium hub airports. Eligibility requires a principal terminal built before 1990 that hasn’t undergone comprehensive redevelopment since then, plus a project with environmental review complete and final design underway. The Transportation Secretary picks the recipients. The bill’s sponsor is a Missouri senator. At St. Louis airport last month, Duffy was asked whether the program appeared tailor made for the airport’s single terminal project. His answer: “That’s a fair assessment.” It’s not even clear whether other airports even qualify given the Rube Goldbergesque rules in the bill. It’s pure pork barrel spending. The same local report notes that Southwest Airlines, which operates more than half of Lambert’s flights, would otherwise bear the largest share of the terminal project’s cost. Moving that bill to federal taxpayers is a windfall for Southwest. The separate $3 billion airport grant pot also bypasses normal allocation formulas and minimum shares. Politicians get more discretion over where the money goes. Bundling that with air traffic control improvements makes it easier to portray objections to the airport spending as opposition to aviation safety. The FAA Has Already Been Spending Billions Congress provided roughly $12.5 billion in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act last year, also from taxpayers rather than airlines and passengers. That came on top of billions in earlier modernization spending largely lit on fire. The Transportation Department’s inspector general reports that the FAA spent more than $15 billion on NextGen through the end of 2024. The effort began in 2003, with completion originally envisioned for 2025. Major capabilities slipped to 2030 or later, costs rose, and the agency reduced what it would deliver. There are improvements underway. Duffy says 69% of copper communications have been replaced and electronic flight strips are installed at 25 towers. But he also acknowledged the FAA’s history during Saturday’s briefing: “They haven’t spent the money well.” Secretary Sean Duffy’s November 14 briefing on the ground stop and modernization funding The FAA set out a plan in 1983 “to equip 150 to 250 airport control towers by 2000.” They went way over budget and didn’t accomplish much. Meanwhile, all of Nav Canada facilities went electronic 15 years ago (and all control towers and TRACONs even earlier). Their solution is used in Australia, Italy, the U.K. and Dubai. We could license the Canadian solution, or other commercial ones, but instead the FAA has been contracting for their own solution since three years before the Beastie Boys were fighting for your right to party. Wait until you explain paper flight strips!https://t.co/fyU7aSILWr pic.twitter.com/gOBIHME3oK — gary leff (@garyleff) July 2, 2023 Modernize The Organization That Runs Air Traffic Control When I reviewed the administration’s plan in May 2025, my concern was that the same institution that had failed to deliver for decades would be asked to execute another enormous upgrade, faster, without fixing its underlying incentives. And there wasn’t a plan to make real changes there. I’ve laid out the Canadian alternative. NAV CANADA has operated since 1996 as a private nonprofit without equity shareholders. It funds operations and capital investment through customer charges and issuing bonds for long-term investments. Transport Canada regulates its safety. Commercial airlines elect four of its 15 directors. Government, employees, general aviation and independent directors also have roles. There’s no need to hand the system to an airline monopoly to get it out of congressional budgeting. The FAA, by contrast, regulates itself – which is a recipe for unaccountability. An outside regulator would have a clearer job: demand safe performance from an operator whose failures it isn’t also responsible for defending. Secretary Sean Duffy’s November 14 briefing on the ground stop and modernization funding

The FAA set out a plan in 1983 “to equip 150 to 250 airport control towers by 2000.” They went way over budget and didn’t accomplish much. Meanwhile, all of Nav Canada facilities went electronic 15 years ago (and all control towers and TRACONs even earlier). Their solution is used in Australia, Italy, the U.K. and Dubai. We could license the Canadian solution, or other commercial ones, but instead the FAA has been contracting for their own solution since three years before the Beastie Boys were fighting for your right to party.

Wait until you explain paper flight strips!https://t.co/fyU7aSILWr pic.twitter.com/gOBIHME3oK

When I reviewed the administration’s plan in May 2025, my concern was that the same institution that had failed to deliver for decades would be asked to execute another enormous upgrade, faster, without fixing its underlying incentives. And there wasn’t a plan to make real changes there. I’ve laid out the Canadian alternative. NAV CANADA has operated since 1996 as a private nonprofit without equity shareholders. It funds operations and capital investment through customer charges and issuing bonds for long-term investments. Transport Canada regulates its safety. Commercial airlines elect four of its 15 directors. Government, employees, general aviation and independent directors also have roles. There’s no need to hand the system to an airline monopoly to get it out of congressional budgeting. The FAA, by contrast, regulates itself – which is a recipe for unaccountability. An outside regulator would have a clearer job: demand safe performance from an operator whose failures it isn’t also responsible for defending. This is elite legislation and is a great example of how it should be done.

Democrats love free money and corruption.

More grift for Duffy’s son in law….and his campaign donors. Years ago, they used to set up some fake companies and a bunch of intermediaries to distance themselves from the money and being too obvious. Now, they’re not even trying to hide the corruption. A lot of controllers are saying the nationwide shutdown was nowhere necessary and most centers were fine. This is just a way to ram through the 50B before the new congress in January. I don’t believe any “official” statements at this point.

If it was “just” maintenance, that’s one thing, but if it had been as a result of a bungled update (this was another theory floating around), I’d say we were getting to the point of “just do an RFP for replacing the equipment with identical capabilities and abandon the modernization program”. Most of the ATC issues seem to be related to headcount, so I’m not sure that an as-is replacement wouldn’t be a better choice (operationally) than the “upgrade”.

Frankly, and ironically, Congress just killing off the push once and for all might be constructive – it would be nice to see agencies face a reality that they /can/ lose the shiny new toy.

@CHRIS gets it. That’s the part that’s so appalling. There should be prosecutions over this.

@Walter Barry — Painfully close…if only you’d said Republicans, since 2016, specifically.

Gary, upon further review, I think you should just admit it: this is your monthly rotating ATC privatization push (NAV CANADA!) with a few high-profile current events spliced in (the recent FAA outage). I see it for what it is—a rhetorical two-step and an ideological leap.

How ironic (and sad) that you’d try to pitch private-sector efficiency as the cure when Friday’s outage literally happened during routine maintenance by a private contractor (L3Harris) on a network they already build and operate.

Kudos for calling out the $18 billion in airport terminal “pork” tacked onto S. 5572. However, using that legislative logrolling to argue we should privatize U.S. air traffic control is absurd.

As I’ve said each time before, we can’t copy-paste NAV CANADA onto a US system with vastly higher traffic volume, complex metroplexes, and heavy military/GA integration without creating a governance structure that major airlines will inevitably bend to their own advantage—at the expense of smaller communities, competition, and workforce stability.

Fix the staffing and modernize the tech with real public accountability; don’t hand the keys to a corporate oligopoly.

There are two fundamental ways to fix ATC problems: Increase capacity or reduce traffic volume (bigger planes, fewer flights, higher airfares, more focus on travel alternatives).

All things considered, I strongly suspect we will wind up with the latter.

@Denver Refugee — Nice false choice you got there. It would be a shame for the status quo if there was actually another way—such as stable long-term funding, hardened backup networks, modern automation platforms, and proper controller staffing. But then again, if the system actually worked, the people benefiting from the dysfunction wouldn’t have an excuse to pitch privatization, would they?

“That’s $12.1 billion for air traffic control systems and facilities, versus $18 billion for airports. About 40% goes to air traffic control.”.

I fly a lot. Antiquated airport equipment is scary. Government is crazy inefficient (see the second avenue subway in New York City). I would be happy to get $12 billion in air traffic control, no matter how much pork is needed to get it.

As humor, I have credit cards (Chase Sapphire Reserve for example) where I receive only 40% benefits for my fees.

@Tomri — “A strange game. The only winning move is not to play…”

I mentioned here before I was flying from JFK to SFO. In SFO, the plane almost landed, Really almost. I was looking almost level at ground equipment from my window. Suddenly the plane lifted steeply and did a go around. The pilot later mentioned airport congestion. I personally think the controller gave him permission to land, but he saw something on the runway when he tried to land. Pilot might have saved my life and everyone on the plane. Air traffic control, especially at major busy airports like SFO needs to improve. Personally, I don’t care what it costs or who does it.

WTH. AOC, if you become President, please modernize traffic control.

@Other Just Saying — Comparing ATC upgrades to the Second Avenue Subway is a huge false equivalence and a major oversimplification as well… that said, phase 2 by 2023! *holding breath* (@Peter?!)

Getting a great deal on a cruise is getting harder. Strong demand for cruises allows cruise lines to raise fares significantly and cut back on last-minute discounts to fill unsold cabins.

As a result, the fares you’ll find for cruises can sometimes be much higher — by 20% or more — than what you were expecting.

So, how do you get the best cruise deal if you’re trying to book a cruise for this year and beyond? To start: Don’t panic. Even if fares seem high, you can find ways to save when booking a vacation at sea.

Below, we’ve assembled 10 of our top tips for finding a bargain on a cruise. These are travel hacks that can work any time — not just when fares are rising. Combine a few of these strategies, and you are sure to find the best cruise deals available on your next sailing.

As is the case for resorts on land, floating resorts (i.e., cruise ships) can be significantly less expensive during the “offseason” travel months of September, October and November.

These are months when kids are typically back in school and family travel drops off, resulting in diminished demand for many types of travel, including cruises.

These months also fall during the Caribbean's hurricane season, which keeps some people away from land resorts and cruise ships in the region.

Related: Cruising during hurricane season: What to know — and should you go?

In addition to the fall months, the offseason period for cruising generally includes parts of January and February, but it varies by region.

Traditionally, the summer months of June, July and August have been high season in many cruise destinations like the Caribbean, Europe and Alaska. The periods around major holidays — such as Easter, Thanksgiving, Christmas and New Year’s Day — also are considered the busy season for cruising and bring higher prices.

It’s a growing truism of the cruise world: The earlier you book, the better price you’ll get.

Cruise lines often open departures for bookings with the lowest prices at which they want to sell the trips. Then, as the departures start filling up, they slowly raise prices on the remaining inventory.

To get the best price on any particular sailing, your best bet, in many cases, is to book right when the sailing opens for sale. This means planning way in advance. Many cruise lines open their reservations for sailings two or even three years before departure.

Booking far in advance can pay off in more ways than one. One big advantage to booking ahead of time is that you’re far more likely to get the exact cabin type you want. On many ships, the least expensive cabins and most expensive suites often sell out first and quickly.

Related: A beginners guide to picking a cruise line

Worried you might miss out on a deal by booking a cruise super far in advance? Here’s the good news: If, for some reason, the cost of your cruise drops at a later date, you often can get your fare reduced to match the lower price (see, Monitor Your Fare, below).

As noted above, cruise lines typically offer their lowest fare for any given sailing just after it opens for booking — often two or even three years before it’s scheduled to begin.

Generally, the fare will only go up as the sailing date approaches, but, in some cases, cruise lines will drop the price of a cruise significantly at the last minute. This can happen when the line finds itself with a lot of unsold cabins for a voyage.

If you’re flexible and can travel on short notice, you can sometimes find a last-minute deal for a cruise where the line is scrambling to fill berths just before a departure.

A key thing to know here is that last-minute discounting isn’t as common as it used to be. Like airlines, cruise lines have become much more savvy about revenue management over the years, and it’s rarer that they find themselves with a lot of unsold inventory on sailings just before departure.

You’ll also have to be flexible to take advantage of these deals. If you have a specific cabin type on a specific sailing on a specific ship that you’re eyeing for a vacation, you can’t count on it being available — especially not at a rock-bottom rate.

Also, don’t forget that you may pay a lot more for flights to a cruise and a precruise hotel if you wait until the last minute to book them. Last-minute cruise deals often work best for travelers who live near a departure port that they can reach easily by car, avoiding the cost of last-minute flights and hotels.

Booking early doesn't mean you've locked in the lowest fare. Cruise lines use dynamic pricing. Fares can rise or fall even after you book, so it pays to keep an eye on prices.

If the fare drops for the same sailing and cabin category, you may be able to get the lower price.

This is often the case until the last few months before the sailing begins, when the cruise enters what’s known as the final payment window. At that point, the fare you’ve paid is locked in.

Cruise lines won't necessarily adjust your booking automatically — you'll need to ask. Policies vary by line. Many of the big lines — including Royal Caribbean, Carnival, Norwegian and Princess — have some form of price-protection or “best price guarantee” program.

Most times, you can reprice your booking at the lower fare before making your final payment. After final payment, your options narrow. Some lines will offer an upgrade, onboard credit or a future cruise credit equal to the difference, rather than cash.

To request a price adjustment, contact the cruise line or your travel agent with your booking number and details of the lower fare. Make sure you're comparing the same sailing and cabin category, and note that not all fare types allow for changes to the fare you’ve paid after booking.

Read the fine print, too. Repricing can mean giving up promotions tied to your original booking, such as onboard credit —  and some lines exclude shorter sailings.

Some cruise-specialist travel agents will monitor your fare for you. You can also set up fare alerts that will send you an email if the price has dropped.

At many big lines, you’ll find that the newest, most amenity-filled cruise ships sell at a premium price. Older ships come with a discount.

The older ships are, of course, older, and they sometimes don’t have quite as much to offer on board as the newer ships. But if you’re looking for a deal, they can bring great value.

If you're not fussy about where you sleep, there's another way to trim your fare. That's booking a guarantee cabin.

A guarantee fare lets you choose the category — inside, oceanview, balcony or suite — but not the specific cabin. The line assigns your room later, sometimes just days before sailing. What you're guaranteed is a cabin in the category you paid for, or a better one.

In return for that flexibility, lines often price guarantee cabins below the cheapest cabin you can pick yourself in the same category. The savings vary by line, sailing and category, but can run from roughly $50 to $200 or more per person.

That's the trade-off: You give up control over deck and location. You could land near the elevators or a noisy venue. If you need a specific spot — close to the dining room for mobility reasons, adjoining cabins for a family or midship if you're prone to seasickness — book a cabin you choose yourself.

Occasionally, when a ship is full in your category, a guarantee passenger sometimes gets bumped up to a better one. This is the exception, rather than the rule. Plenty of guarantee bookings end up in the least desirable cabin in the category.

Are you a plan-it-yourself type of traveler? We get it. Many of TPG’s staffers are that way, too.

But even if you book all your land trips on your own, you might want to use a travel agent who is a cruise specialist to book your next voyage.

One big reason is that cruise-selling travel agents often have access to lower bulk fares for sailings that aren’t available to the general public. Big travel agencies will block out large chunks of cabins on ships soon after they open for booking to lock in such group fares, then sell them over the coming months.

When you book through cruise travel agents, you can sometimes receive lower fares and extra perks like onboard credit or amenities.

Travel agents specializing in cruising will also be able to guide you through the many types of cabin categories on some cruise ships and steer you away from cabins to avoid. Plus, they’ll be there for you when things go wrong on a cruise.

You don't have to be planning an extended family reunion or large event to get a group deal. Most cruise lines treat a booking of several cabins as a group — and they reward it.

The threshold varies by line; eight cabins is common, though some lines start lower. Perks can include a discounted group fare, onboard credit and, for the person who organizes the booking, a free berth. That's essentially one free fare, not including taxes and fees. The bigger the group, the bigger the perks.

Even if you aren't traveling with a crowd, it's possible to build one. Cruise forums and social media groups often organize sailing-specific meetups where strangers pool cabins under a single group booking to reach the threshold. Each cabin typically pays its own fare, and some organizers pass part of the savings along to the group.

Group bookings can come with their own payment schedules and change or cancellation rules, so read the terms before you commit. These bookings usually run through a cruise-specialist travel agent or the line's group desk.

Some of the best bargains in the cruise world are the voyages that cruise ships make as they reposition from one part of the world to another.

This is because cruise lines often have trouble selling these trips. They typically have oddball itineraries with very few port calls and lots of sea days — something that doesn’t appeal to many cruisers. Repositioning cruises also tend to be considerably longer than standard weekend getaways or weeklong voyages — a turnoff to the many travelers who have limited vacation days.

To sell them, cruise lines often have to reduce their per-day prices sharply, making them a bargain.

Among the most common repositioning cruises are sailings between the Caribbean and Europe in the spring as lines move ships to Europe for the summer. Similarly, there’s a wave of repositioning cruises between Europe and the Caribbean in the fall.

You’ll also find some repositioning cruises every year between the Caribbean and Alaska and between the West Coast and Asia or Australia.

Some cruise lines offer reduced fares or special perks to special groups, these include military members and veterans, teachers, seniors and residents of particular states or regions.

Terms vary widely. Eligibility for spouses, age cutoffs and whether the discount can be combined with other promotions all differ by line, so ask when you book and have your documentation ready.

#6058. You Can Transfer British Airways Avios To Someone Else For $11 Using The Finnair Loophole

British Airways charges most members £50 per transaction to give Avios to someone else, and each transfer tops out at 60,000 points. Move the same points through Finnair and you can give someone 100,000 Avios for a single €10 fee. You can move British Airways Avios into a Finnair account, and Finnair charges €10 to transfer Avios to another member. I’ve written about moving Avios between airline programs to get the best redemption deal. The same flexibility lets you choose which program’s rules to use when giving points to another person. For two people with British Airways balances, the process is: Each person links their own British Airways and Finnair accounts. Names and email addresses need to match within each person’s accounts, and both programs need two-factor authentication enabled. The person giving the points moves their Avios into their own Finnair account. That transfer is free and 1:1. They use Finnair Shop’s transfer function to send the Avios to the other person’s Finnair account, paying €10. The recipient can use the points through Finnair or move them into their own linked British Airways account, again free at 1:1. Under the British Airways transfer terms, sending 100,000 Avios takes two transactions at £50 apiece, or the equivalent charged in your home currency (Gold members are exempt from that fee). Senders and recipients are each limited to 200,000 Avios per calendar year. Finnair doesn’t cap the amount or frequency of member transfers beyond your available balance. However, moving the points between airlines has its own limits. Open the accounts in advance. Finnair requires an account to be at least 30 days old to link with another Avios program. The sender must have been a member for at least 90 days to transfer to another person online. Finnair allows newer members to transfer via customer care at a higher €20 transfer fee. This route is for adults. Linking requires members to be at least 18, and you can’t transfer Avios into a Finnair Plus Junior account. Transfer ceiling. Finnair allows 1–999,999 Avios per cross-program transaction. Basic members have a shared 1 million Avios limit over 12 months, counting all linked programs and both directions. Higher tiers don’t have that 12-month cap. You may not need to pay anything. British Airways’ free household account pools balances for redemptions, and you can often simply book an award for someone else. But this lets you do it without restricting redemptions from your account to members of your household account. Don’t leave the points sitting in a dormant Finnair account. Transfers don’t restart their 18-month expiration clock. One Reddit member reported losing newly transferred Avios less than two weeks later because the Finnair account was already inactive. They subsequently reported getting the points back after contacting the airline. Topics on this pageAviosBritish AirwaysFinnairLoyalty programReddit+1 more More From View from the Wing

Finnair doesn’t cap the amount or frequency of member transfers beyond your available balance. However, moving the points between airlines has its own limits.

You may not need to pay anything. British Airways’ free household account pools balances for redemptions, and you can often simply book an award for someone else. But this lets you do it without restricting redemptions from your account to members of your household account.

Don’t leave the points sitting in a dormant Finnair account. Transfers don’t restart their 18-month expiration clock. They subsequently reported getting the points back after contacting the airline.

There shouldn’t need to be loopholes for this. Transferring points you already own should be free. We ought to properly regulate these corporate pseudocurrencies to include basic consumer protections—like free transfers, advance notice for program changes, and stabilized values—so these stealth devaluations stop. You’d think the banks underwriting these multi-billion-dollar currencies would want stability, too, before constant devaluations burn out the consumers fueling their credit card portfolios.

Wasn’t there an old Court case involving UA and a customer over the “meaning” of lifetime membership in their Club? If memory serves, the court sided with airline saying lifetime is what the airline says. What you describes a similar case.

The 30-day account age rule is the part I’d flag for anyone trying this in a hurry — you really do need to set the Finnair accounts up well ahead of time. The expiry warning matters too: moving points doesn’t restart that 18-month clock, so it’s worth checking the receiving account is active before sending a large balance across. For smaller gifts, the household account route Gary mentions is probably simpler, but for a one-off larger transfer this €10 path is hard to beat.

@alanZ — H’yup. Lagen v. United Continental Holdings. Flyer spent years working towards United’s million-miler program, which promised ‘premier executive’ status. But, when United merged with Continental, and slashed those perks, he sued for breach of contract. 7th Circuit sided with airline, citing MileagePlus rules, which gave United the unilateral right to modify, devalue, or terminate program benefits “on a whim” with or without notice. I prefer Judge Hamilton’s dissent, which notes an airline’s definition of ‘lifetime’ means: “Lifetime, unless we change our mind.” So, like I’ve been saying, we can close this regulatory vacuum, if we wanted, but we haven’t in the US at least for now.

One of the best reasons to apply for a travel rewards card is the welcome offer. By hitting certain minimum spending requirements, you can often earn tens or even hundreds of thousands of points or miles within the first few months of opening a card.

But welcome offers change frequently, and knowing when to apply can make a big difference. After all, you don't want to miss out on bonus points by applying too early or too late.

To help you determine whether an offer is worth pursuing, we've compiled the welcome offer histories of several popular American Express cards, along with our recommendations for when to apply.

Apply now for the American Express Platinum Card®: Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 175,000 bonus points after spending $8,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

You can also check our frequently updated list of the best increased card offers currently available.

Here are some of the most popular Amex cards, with guidance on when you should apply for each.

While American Express offers several types of welcome bonuses, we’re only discussing publicly available welcome offers.

Public offers are generally available to eligible applicants, while targeted offers are extended to select individuals and may feature higher bonuses or different spending requirements.

Amex also uses personalized bonuses on certain cards, allowing applicants to see which welcome offer they're eligible for before deciding whether to accept the card. The advertised "as high as" amount represents the maximum potential bonus, not necessarily what every applicant will receive. Additionally, offers may change at any time, and some of the offers mentioned below may not be available.

Keep in mind that American Express only allows you to earn one bonus per lifetime on each of its cards, so make sure to wait for the best time to apply. In addition, you may not be eligible for a welcome offer if you've already held a higher-tier card in the same family.

For example, if you currently have or have previously held the American Express Platinum Card®, you may not be eligible for a welcome offer on the American Express® Gold Card.

Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 100,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

The Amex Platinum has long been one of the most popular premium cards on the market, despite its steep $895 annual fee (see rates and fees).

It offers a slew of luxury-skewing, value-added benefits that can save cardmembers money on everything from airline fees to hotel stays.

Here are the offers we have seen on the Amex Platinum:

*Valuations are based on TPG's November 2026 valuations and are not from the issuer.

When the Amex Platinum ran its highest-ever offer, applicants could find out their offer and see if they were eligible for as high as 175,000 bonus points after spending $8,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Offer no longer available; welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

Generally, apply for this card only if you can secure a welcome offer of 150,000 points or more, whether through a targeted or limited-time offer.

The Amex Business Platinum often extends even more lucrative welcome offers than its personal counterpart and offers many of the same luxury perks, though some of its statement credits are focused on typical business expenditures.

Cardmembers pay the same $895 annual fee for the Business Platinum (see rates and fees) as the consumer Platinum.

Here are the offers we have seen on the Amex Business Platinum:

*Valuations are based on TPG's valuations and are not from the issuer.

With the current welcome offer on the Amex Business Platinum, you may be eligible for as high as 300,000 bonus points after spending $20,000 on purchases in the first three months of card membership. (Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.) If you receive an offer for the full 300,000 points, that's by far the best we've seen.

Any time this card’s welcome offer equals or tops 200,000 points, it’s worth considering.

Learn more: American Express Business Platinum

The Amex Gold is an excellent everyday choice for foodies since it earns 4 points per dollar spent at restaurants worldwide on up to $50,000 per calendar year (then 1 point per dollar spent thereafter) and on up to $25,000 per calendar year at U.S. supermarkets (then 1 point per dollar spent). These are solid earning rates for a card with a $325 annual fee (see rates and fees).

Here are the offers we have seen on the Amex Gold:

*Valuations are based on TPG's valuations and are not from the issuer.

New applicants could find out their offer and see if they were eligible for as high as 100,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Offer no longer available; welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

If you're able to get at least 60,000 points in your offer, it's worth applying.

The Amex Business Gold card is great for small businesses thanks to its strong earning structure. It earns 4 points per dollar spent on your top two eligible spending categories each billing cycle (up to $150,000 per calendar year; then 1 point per dollar spent). Cardmembers pay $375 each year to hold this card (see rates and fees).

Here are the offers we've seen on the Amex Business Gold:

*Valuations are based on TPG's valuations and are not from the issuer.

With the current welcome offer, new cardmembers may be eligible for as high as 200,000 bonus points after spending $15,000 on purchases in the first three months of card membership. (Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

If you see an offer for this card with 100,000 points or more and a spending requirement that you and your small business can easily meet, it’s worth applying.

Learn more: American Express Business Gold

The American Express Graphite Card carries a $295 annual fee (see rates and fees) and is aimed at high-spending businesses that want to earn cash back with American Express.

While we can't say for certain what future offers on the Amex Graphite Card will look like, we encourage you to apply for the current offer if you're interested in the card.

The Blue Cash Preferred is one of the best cash-back cards currently available, with high 6% cash back earning rates on U.S. streaming subscriptions and U.S. supermarkets (U.S. supermarkets are subject to a $6,000 spending cap per calendar year, then 1%; users receive cash back in the form of Reward Dollars that they can redeem as a statement credit and at Amazon.com checkout.)

The card has a $0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $95 annually thereafter (see rates and fees).

Here are the offers we have seen on the Amex Blue Cash Preferred:

This card’s welcome offer doesn’t vary much, but currently new cardmembers may be eligible for as high as $300 cash back after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer; Cash back is received as Reward Dollars that can be redeemed for a statement credit or for other select options.)

Consider applying if you're eligible for an offer of at least $250 cash back.

Learn more: American Express Blue Cash Preferred

Though its earnings aren’t as solid as those of the Blue Cash Preferred, the Blue Cash Everyday still earns cash back at a steady rate. This card's lower earning rates are understandable, given that it has no annual fee (see rates and fees).

(Users receive cash back in the form of Reward Dollars that they can redeem as a statement credit and at Amazon.com checkout.)

Here are the offers we have seen on the Amex Blue Cash Everyday:

When the Blue Cash Everyday had its highest offer, new cardmembers could earn $200 cash back after spending $2,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership (no longer available).

Go for an offer with at least a $200 cash-back bonus.

Learn more: American Express Blue Cash Everyday

American Express is the sole issuer of Delta's cobranded consumer and business cards. Amex's Delta cards feature elevated offers more commonly than most of their proprietary cards, so it's very important to know when it's the right time to apply.

If you're interested in one of Amex's Delta cards, check out our guide on Delta's cards' offer history to help you decide when it's the best time to apply.

American Express offers a range of cobranded Hilton cards to suit every traveler, from beginners to hardcore Hilton loyalists. Like Amex's Delta cards, the Hilton cards receive elevated welcome offers more frequently than the cards we've featured in this guide.

If you're interested in one of Amex's Hilton cards, we have a guide on when it's best to apply, based on the offer history of all Hilton cards.

Marriott's portfolio of cards can be more challenging to track because it includes cards issued by Chase and American Express. The two issuers don't necessarily put elevated offers on their Marriott cards at the same time. Plus, both issuers have their own application rules and restrictions.

If you're interested in one of Amex's Marriott cards, we have a guide to the offer history of all Marriott cards to help you know when it's the right time to apply.

Pay attention to the welcome offers of any travel rewards cards you may be interested in, as offers can change frequently. Applying at the wrong time could mean missing out on thousands of bonus points or hundreds of dollars in cash back.

Before applying for any new card, look at the range of its previous welcome offers. Then, when an offer hits the higher end of that range, you can feel sure you’re getting a great deal and making the right choice for your rewards strategy.

#6055. New Hyatt Credit Card Offer: Earn 4 Free Nights—Why I Spend On The Card Towards Elite Status

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

The World Of Hyatt Credit Card (See rates and fees) has a new initial bonus: earn 4 free nights at any Category 1-4 Hyatt hotel or resort after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. That’s an improved offer from a card whose bonuses have usually been more modest than competing travel cards.

I have this card, and I put actual spending on it. Hyatt points are still valuable, but what gets me to use the card is the credit toward elite status and the rewards earned along the way. Hyatt status does more to improve my hotel stays than status with other major chains.

These are four separate certificates, so you can use them for one trip or spread them across different stays. You’ll need standard room award availability, and the certificates expire 12 months after they’re issued. The terms require checkout before the expiration date. Under Hyatt’s current award chart, a Category 4 standard room can cost as much as 25,000 points per night. Four certificates could therefore cover nights that would otherwise require 100,000 points. Their category restrictions and expiration date make them less flexible than having those points in your account. The card has a $95 annual fee. Chase excludes current holders of this card and previous cardmembers who received its initial bonus within the past 24 months. The usual Chase restriction on applicants who’ve opened five or more personal cards in the past 24 months also generally applies. Why I Keep The Card And Spend On It The annual Category 1-4 free night after each cardmember anniversary makes the $95 fee easy to justify. There’s also a second Category 1-4 night after $15,000 in purchases during a calendar year which makes that spending more rewarding. And these nights are transferable to another World of Hyatt member. If I won’t use one, I can give it to someone who will. For spending, the card earns 4 Hyatt points per dollar on qualifying Hyatt purchases; 2 on restaurants, airline tickets bought directly from airlines, local transit and commuting, and fitness club and gym memberships; and 1 on other purchases. More significantly, it comes with 5 qualifying nights each year, plus 2 more qualifying nights for every $5,000 spent. Those nights count toward both status and Milestone Rewards. Put $15,000 of otherwise unbonused spending on the card during a calendar year and you earn: 15,000 Hyatt points. An additional Category 1-4 free night certificate. 6 qualifying nights from spending, giving you 11 including the card’s annual 5. That means 49 qualifying nights actually spent in hotels, plus the card’s 5 annual nights and 6 from spending, gets you to the 60 needed for Globalist. And the $5,000 spent earning the initial bonus counts toward the $15,000 free-night threshold in the calendar year when you spend it. Milestone Rewards start at 20 qualifying nights and continue every 10 nights through 150. Some of the rewards on the way to Globalist are: Qualifying Nights Notable Rewards 30 A Category 1-4 free night, plus a choice of additional reward. 40 A Guest of Honor Award, plus a choice that includes a Suite Upgrade Award. 50 A choice that includes 2 Suite Upgrade Awards. 60 Globalist status, a Category 1-7 free night, 2 Suite Upgrade Awards, 2 Guest of Honor Awards, and My Hyatt Concierge. The value of another $5,000 in spending depends on where those two nights get me. Crossing a threshold for suite upgrades or Globalist can be worth giving up a higher earning rate on another card. Hyatt Status Is Stronger Than At Other Major Chains The card itself comes with Discoverist status. That’s better than a hole in the head as my grandfather used to say. But reaching Globalist has real value – as well as the milestone choices along the way. The biggest benefit is confirming a suite at the time of booking with a Suite Upgrade Award for up to seven nights when an eligible standard suite is available for the stay. That’s a huge value on family trips. I also value having a My Hyatt Concierge I can email requests to, actual delivery of 4 p.m. late checkout at eligible properties, and a more generous breakfast benefit than I get from other chains. At participating hotels without an available club lounge, Globalist breakfast generally covers a full breakfast for up to two adults and two children registered in the room, including tax and gratuity. Late checkout has exceptions, including availability limits at resorts, but I’m usually proactively offered late checkout everywhere else (and personally find it honored more often than not at resorts). The Free Night Certificates Should Be More Flexible The current version of this card launched in 2018. Its annual certificate is still capped at Category 4, while category creep has taken away many of the hotels where I’d most want to use it. Just this year, 14 hotels moved from Category 4 to Category 5, including Hyatt Regency Seattle, Hyatt Regency Grand Cypress and Hyatt Regency Jersey City. Five moved the other way, bringing options like Hyatt Centric Congress Avenue Austin and Dream Nashville within reach, but the certificate lost more hotels than it gained. I’d like Hyatt to at least let members add points to a certificate to book a higher category. The certificate works at a Category 4 hotel charging 25,000 points, but won’t work at a Category 5 hotel when it’s charging 15,000 points. And I wish Hyatt would let us combine these free nights with Suite Upgrade Awards or Guest of Honor Awards. I value them most traveling with my family when I’m paying for rooms out of pocket. That’s always when I want to use my suite upgrades! I don’t need a suite on a business stay (paid by someone else, when it’s just me) or to use the free night award. @nsx at FlyerTalk gets it. Only outsized value I ever got on one of those was Park Hyatt in Doha, and there’s no freaking way I’m routing through there again anytime soon. Hyatt (and Chase) are long-overdue for an actual premium co-branded credit card product that includes either an uncapped or up to Cat 8 free night for a $500+ AF.

Cat 1-4 with Hyatt is useless. Got five 50k free nights (which can be topped up) for getting the Marriott card and was able to put those to good use.

How Hyatt has fallen when a Marriott offer is better than one of their’s.

I’ve gotten great value with the category 1- 4 free night awards in Asia.

I have a suggestion: Allow us to use two Cat 4 free nights for one Cat 8 free night. Because 2×4=8.

@nsx at FlyerTalk – Math and logic checks out.

@1990 – GTV VI before a Hyatt premium card? Wild!

If it is anything like the initial partnership with American (which I miss), the upcoming partnership with Delta should add even more value to using the Hyatt card, staying at Hyatt, and reaching Hyatt milestones and status.

@john — Almost forgot about that switcharoo. RIP AA-Hyatt partnership.

@L737 — “Hopefully things will turn around and get better in November…” (dog poop can be used as a melee weapon?!)

This would have some muscle even if they allowed Cat 5. But Cat 1-4 is basically 4 star futility at this point.

@BBT — For real. Though, coincidentally, all the decent properties would be elevated to Category 6, overnight. Grand Hyatt at SFO? Naw, we a Cat 6 now…

When I got this card a few years ago, the offer was for two nights – but without the category 1-4 restriction. I remember using the two free nights to stay at the Park Hyatt in Manhattan, which was a good use of those two free nights.

I think 4 nights in category 1-4 is a devaluatuon

Speaking of hotel brands… @L737, did you see Wendover’s video today?

Agree the cap stings, but 4 certs still work well for the boring nights that add up, airport stays, a road trip stopover or a Hyatt Place in a secondary city where cash rates spike on event weekends. The trick is checking the cash price of that exact night before you burn one, sometimes it’s only $120 and the cert is better saved. FWIW a free tool like HotelPriceTracker emails you when a rate drops, so you get a feel for what a night really costs over a few weeks. IMO if you’d use 2 of the 4 the card pays for itself, if not skip it

I think the category creep is happening across the hotel credit cards. Bonvoy now allows you to top up the points on their “free night” from the included 80,000 all the way up to 100K. Coincidentally, check out how many hotels seem to require 103K points for redemption.

I think Hyatt could also benefit from a more premium card. I’d pay the $800 fee for a higher level card like Hilton and Marriott offer. Have it include a Category 7 or 8 night, get me Explorist, and a path to Globalist. I’d sign up or upgrade in a minute

#6054. Trump says no Iran deal needed after conflict drove GOP’s midterm losses

President Donald Trump on Thursday shut down his administration’s on-again-off-again talks with Iran, saying he would not seek a deal to formally end the nine-month-old conflict with Tehran.

The possible end of the pursuit of a diplomatic solution came nine days after Trump and congressional Republicans suffered massive losses in the midterm elections. House Democrats will have more than 250 seats come January, and Senate Democrats will have at least 55 seats in the Senate — with Alaska’s competitive race still uncalled.

Polls leading up to Election Day and since have shown that a majority of voters, and a sizeable chunk of Trump’s Republican base, felt the Iran conflict was a mistake.

Vice President JD Vance penned a lengthy social media post the day after the election, blaming, in large part, the Iran war for the coast-to-coast Democratic victories. Some GOP lawmakers have also called for an end to the conflict, which drove up fuel and other commodity prices.

"The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote the morning after the GOP wipeout. "The president himself said so last night."

Trump has said that he agrees with Vance’s assessment but that if he had to decide again whether to join Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in striking Iranian targets, he would reach the same conclusion. On Monday, he told reporters that the Iran war "militarily is effectively over."

Vance had been Trump’s designated top negotiator in the talks with Iran’s remaining leaders, but the president said Thursday on social media that he had ordered his second-in-command to instead “focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S.”

“We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed,” he added. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!"

The situation along the Strait of Hormuz remains contested and dangerous for commercial vessels, including ones that deliver a large amount of the world’s oil products. Iranian officials contend that they control most of the key waterway.

Trump, Vance and other administration officials have said in recent weeks that they were open to continuing talks with Iran, while criticizing Tehran's negotiating tactics. Last week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who also is Trump’s national security adviser, told reporters that Iran's latest demands were unreasonable.

Trump’s announcement Thursday could represent his latest way to try assuaging GOP voters, including members of his “Make America Great Again” base. A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted after the midterms and released Tuesday showed that a majority of Republicans (51 percent) want Congress to pass legislation that would end the Iran conflict. Overall, 71 percent of Americans would support such a bill, the survey found.

The conflict was front-and-center during the midterms campaign.

Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers, who lost the Senate race in Michigan to Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, called for the Iran conflict to end "quickly."

“Michigan families are struggling with the price of everyday life. Groceries cost too much. We have to bring prices down," Rogers said in one campaign ad.

On Capitol Hill, GOP lawmakers have tried giving Trump cover, while raising some concerns about high gas prices and questioning whether the president and his team have a viable exit strategy.

As the midterms campaign hit the homestretch in late September, two Iowa Republicans in tight races, Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, voted with Democrats on a measure to end the conflict.

“With the negotiating window closed, sustained combat operations now require congressional authorization,” Nunn, an Air Force veteran, wrote on social media. “I will not support another open-ended war.”

Nunn and Miller-Meeks both lost their seats last week, despite breaking with the president over the war.

Trump’s declaration this week of a military end to the Iran war came more than seven years after he offered some foreshadowing during a June 25, 2019, exchange with this CQ Roll Call reporter in the Oval Office.

Asked that day what his exit strategy would be if war ever broke out with Iran, he said: “You’re not going to need an exit strategy. I don’t do exit strategies.”

#6053. The Multi-Billion-Dollar Loyalty Mirage: Why We Still Don’t Know What Airline Cards Really Earn

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: It's uncertain how much money airline credit cards generate.  Grok

United CEO Scott Kirby says investors overestimate airline credit-card profits, but filings from United, Delta, and American show substantial loyalty-program cash flows without establishing what the bank deals actually earn.

Airlines are often called credit card companies that operate planes. United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby rejects that idea.

In an October 27 interview on the Cheeky Pint podcast, Kirby noted that over 50,000 passengers fly United daily on credit card miles. Outside analysts see the cash banks pay for those miles, he argued, but ignore the cost to carry those passengers. “Nobody counts the cost,” he said. “All that we disclose is the revenue.”

It's a fair challenge to a popular argument. But the public filings tell a more complicated story. During the pandemic, United, Delta and American showed lenders how much cash their loyalty programs could produce. And American has since told investors what a bigger bank deal could add to earnings.

The key question is how much of that cash translates into genuine profit. Skift previously analyzed the payment fees funding these travel rewards. Now, we look at the other side of the trade.

United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby pushed back on the idea that airlines are credit card companies with planes attached, telling the Cheeky Pint podcast on October 27 that more than 50,000 passengers fly United daily on credit card miles and that analysts count the revenue from selling miles while ignoring the cost of carrying those passengers. The public filings support part of his point and complicate the rest. Delta reported $8.2 billion from its American Express deal in 2025, up 11%, and American collected $6.2 billion from credit-card and other partners. United does not publish total cash received from banks; it reported $2.7 billion in loyalty marketing and partner-benefit revenue in the first nine months of 2026, up from $2.4 billion, and ended 2025 with about $7.8 billion in deferred loyalty revenue. United's own June 2020 MileagePlus presentation showed a bank paying $300 for 15,000 miles, with MileagePlus paying the airline unit $150 for the seat and recording a 50% margin — but that $150 was an internal transfer price between units of the same parent, not the cost of flying the passenger. Award travel has grown meaningfully: 6.1 million flight awards used in 2019, or 7.2% of passenger miles, versus 10.9 million and 10.3% in 2025. Kirby's 50,000-a-day figure implies more than 18 million passengers a year, and United has not publicly reconciled the gap with its filings.

#6052. 3 Women Stranded By FAA Nationwide Ground Stop Bought A $48,000 Ford Bronco—Then Drove 27 Hours Home

Three women stranded in Charlotte after Friday’s nationwide flight grounding bought a $48,000 Ford Bronco and drove 27 hours home to North Dakota. They’d gone away for work training. They came home with a new car. Tara Harding (I first read this as Tonya Harding) and two employees needed to get back to their families in Bismarck, and had patients to see Monday morning. Tara Harding and her employees were at the airport trying to get home from a work trip when a nationwide ground stop left them stranded in Charlotte, North Carolina — roughly 1,600 miles from home in Bismarck, North Dakota. She found a $48,000 solution in the form of a new Ford Bronco. https://t.co/xpP9fmCsm8 — NBC News (@NBCNews) November 16, 2026 They couldn’t find a rental car within four hours of Charlotte. They tried other ways home, including a train, bus and U-Haul. None worked. Delta Air Lines left them stranded. Harding’s mother-in-law suggested buying a car. They bought the Bronco with no money down. Harding initially planned to sell it to a dealership once they reached home. The women took turns driving and sleeping. While flights resumed at 8:15 p.m. Eastern on Friday, over 18,000 trips were cancelled and there simply weren’t seats to accommodate all passengers on later flights and it took several days to clear everyone out. #6051. Where Have All the Boys’ Books Gone?

When a culture won’t let boys be boys, fiction designed for them goes the way of the dodo.

Covers of Tom Swift and the Visitor from Planet X (left) and the Hardy Boys mystery The Tower Treasure.

NR Illustration; Public Domain/Wikicommons

Discourse on the socials has dredged up an old question again: Why aren’t boys reading books? It was spurred by an Atlantic article a fortnight ago, which suggested that “a lack of male protagonists is making it harder to get young readers into books.” This was denounced, of course. Boys should read about female characters to correct historical imbalances, for one thing. Also, boys reading about female protagonists helps them be empathetic. Also: Ew, boys.

As someone who grew up with a wide variety of boys’ books, let me explain. We didn’t care if there were girls in the books, as long as they didn’t get in the way. This sentiment would get you drummed out of the market today, because how can girls possibly be in the way? They can help! They can solve problems! Yes, absolutely, and they are welcome to do so over there in the Nancy Drew books, where they can solve the Mystery of the Lovesick Horse or whatever. We regarded Nancy Drew as capable and ingenious, pointing a flashlight at a clue, but we had no interest in reading her exploits. Girls just changed things. You had to make sure your shirt was tucked in, and you couldn’t blow your nose by closing a nostril and snorting. If you passed gas, they got prissy instead of laughing and hitting you in the arm, hard, knuckle out, and yes, that hurt but you wouldn’t say anything and you’d get him back later. If you were a Hardy Boy in the woods working on a mystery and you had to relieve yourself, you could walk over to a tree and do it and not worry if you made any noise. In fact, you might actually aim for some broad-leaf flora to amplify your relief.

#6050. Former Maine Gov. Paul LePage declared winner of open House seat

Paul LePage, the former Maine governor who once said he was “Donald Trump before Donald Trump,” is heading to Congress.

The Associated Press called the race for the open 2nd District on Thursday after the Maine Secretary of State’s office tabulated the votes under the state’s ranked choice voting system. LePage ended up ahead of Democratic state Auditor Matt Dunlap 50.8 percent to 49.2 percent.

Dunlap had already conceded the race to LePage, who will succeed retiring Democratic Rep. Jared Golden in the sprawling district, which includes much of Maine outside the Portland and Augusta areas.

“Paul LePage is already hard at work for the people of Maine attending Congressional orientation, meeting with national leaders, and making it clear the political parties need to work together for the American people,” Brent Littlefield, a senior adviser to LePage, said in a statement Thursday. “As Paul said, he will work with anyone, regardless of Party, to put Maine first.”

LePage’s win is a glimmer of good news for Republicans, who saw massive losses across the country in last week’s midterm elections. He is one of three Republicans, along with Texas’ Jace Yarbrough and Tennessee’s Brent Taylor, to have flipped a House seat, although Maine’s 2nd District is the only one of the three that wasn’t redrawn to favor the GOP.

LePage’s win also means that at least one Republican will continue to represent New England in Congress, taking up the mantle from Maine Sen. Susan Collins, who lost her own reelection bid last week.

Golden, who was first elected in 2018, had been a top Republican target throughout his time in Congress. But the lawmaker, known for bucking his party, proved difficult to unseat in the past two election cycles.

“I also know a thing or two about winning in tough circumstances. So, I know you have to tip your hat to Paul LePage for winning in the midst of this Blue Tsunami,” Golden said in a social media post last week.

Dunlap initially launched his campaign as a primary challenge to Golden in the fall of 2025, only for the congressman to announce his retirement a month later. Dunlap went on to win a four-way contest for the Democratic nomination.
